sections.raw_text:
(1) The Court of a Magistrate may award such term of imprisonment in default of payment of fine as is authorised by law:
Provided that the term—
(a) is not in excess of the powers of the Magistrate under section 23;
(b) shall not, where imprisonment has been awarded as part of the substantive sentence, exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment which the Magistrate is competent to inflict as punishment for the offence otherwise than as imprisonment in default of payment of the fine.
(2) The imprisonment awarded under this section may be in addition to a substantive sentence of imprisonment for the maximum term awardable by the Magistrate under section 23.

breakdown.plain_summary: When a Magistrate imposes a fine, the law also authorizes a backstop: imprisonment if the fine goes unpaid. This section caps that default-imprisonment term in two ways — it can never exceed what the Magistrate could impose under Section 23 in the first place, and where the fine is combined with a substantive prison sentence, the default term is additionally capped at one-fourth of the maximum substantive imprisonment that Magistrate could impose for the offence. Sub-section (2) confirms this default-imprisonment term stacks on top of (is additional to) the substantive sentence, up to the Magistrate's maximum under Section 23.
essential_elements: Default imprisonment for unpaid fine is capped by the Magistrate's general sentencing power under Section 23
Where combined with a substantive imprisonment sentence, default imprisonment is additionally capped at one-fourth of the maximum substantive term the Magistrate could impose
Default imprisonment may be awarded in addition to (stacked on top of) the maximum substantive sentence
breakdown.how_to_read: Always run the two-step cap check together: first confirm the default term doesn't exceed the Magistrate's overall Section 23 ceiling, then separately check the one-fourth-of-substantive-term cap if a substantive prison sentence was also imposed — both limits apply simultaneously.

sections.title: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial
sections.raw_text:
(1) When a person is convicted at one trial of two or more offences, the Court may, subject to the provisions of section 9 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, sentence him for such offences, to the several punishments prescribed therefor which such Court is competent to inflict and the Court shall, considering the gravity of offences, order such punishments to run concurrently or consecutively.
(2) In the case of consecutive sentences, it shall not be necessary for the Court by reason only of the aggregate punishment for the several offences being in excess of the punishment which it is competent to inflict on conviction of a single offence, to send the offender for trial before a higher Court:
Provided that—
(a) in no case shall such person be sentenced to imprisonment for a longer period than twenty years;
(b) the aggregate punishment shall not exceed twice the amount of punishment which the Court is competent to inflict for a single offence.
(3) For the purpose of appeal by a convicted person, the aggregate of the consecutive sentences passed against him under this section shall be deemed to be a single sentence.

breakdown.plain_summary: When one trial results in convictions on multiple offences, the Court must decide whether the sentences run concurrently (simultaneously) or consecutively (back-to-back), weighing the gravity of the offences. Consecutive sentencing is allowed to push the aggregate punishment above what the Court could impose for any single offence — without needing to refer the case up to a higher Court purely because the total exceeds the Court's ordinary per-offence ceiling — but two hard limits apply: total imprisonment can never exceed twenty years, and the aggregate cannot exceed twice what the Court could impose for a single offence. For appeal purposes, the combined consecutive sentence is treated as one single sentence, not multiple separate ones.
essential_elements: Applies where one trial results in conviction of two or more offences
Court decides concurrent vs. consecutive sentencing based on gravity of the offences
Consecutive sentencing may push the aggregate above the Court's per-offence ceiling without requiring reference to a higher Court
Hard cap: aggregate imprisonment never exceeds 20 years
Hard cap: aggregate punishment never exceeds twice the Court's per-single-offence competence
For appeal purposes, the aggregate consecutive sentence is deemed a single sentence
exceptions_and_qualifications: The whole section operates subject to Section 9 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (the substantive-law provision on punishment for multiple offences)
breakdown.how_to_read: Apply both caps in sub-section (2) independently — a sentence must satisfy both the absolute 20-year ceiling and the twice-the-single-offence-competence ceiling; whichever is lower actually controls in a given case.

sections.title: Mode of conferring powers
sections.raw_text:
(1) In conferring powers under this Sanhita, the High Court or the State Government, as the case may be, may, by order, empower persons specially by name or in virtue of their offices or classes of officials generally be their official titles.
(2) Every such order shall take effect from the date on which it is communicated to the person so empowered.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section is the mechanical rule for how the High Court or State Government actually hands out powers under the Sanhita: either by naming a specific individual, or more broadly by office/official title (empowering, say, “every Superintendent of Police” as a class, rather than naming each person). Critically, the power doesn't take effect the moment the order is signed — it only takes effect once it is actually communicated to the person being empowered.
essential_elements: Powers may be conferred on named individuals, or generally on holders of a specified office/official title
Empowerment is by order of the High Court or State Government, as applicable
The order takes effect only from the date it is communicated to the empowered person, not from the date it is made
breakdown.how_to_read: Keep the communication-triggers-effect rule in mind whenever a person's exercise of a conferred power is challenged as premature — the operative date is receipt/communication, not issuance.

sections.title: Powers of officers appointed to an equal or higher office
sections.raw_text: Whenever any person holding an office in the service of Government who has been invested by the High Court or the State Government with any powers under this Sanhita throughout any local area is appointed to an equal or higher office of the same nature, within a like local area under the same State Government, he shall, unless the High Court or the State Government, as the case may be, otherwise directs, or has otherwise directed, exercise the same powers in the local area in which he is so appointed.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a continuity rule for government officers who get promoted or transferred within the same State: if an officer already holds Sanhita powers over one local area, and is then appointed to an equal or higher post of the same nature in a similarly-structured local area, he automatically keeps exercising the same powers in his new posting — by default, without needing a fresh empowerment order — unless the High Court or State Government specifically directs otherwise.
essential_elements: Applies to an officer already invested with Sanhita powers in one local area
Who is then appointed to an equal or higher office of the same nature in a like local area under the same State Government
Default rule: the same powers continue automatically in the new posting
Displaced only by a specific contrary direction from the High Court or State Government
exceptions_and_qualifications: Only applies when moving to an equal or higher post of the same nature — a lateral move to a materially different kind of office is not automatically covered
breakdown.how_to_read: This default-continuity rule saves re-empowerment paperwork on ordinary promotions/transfers — but always check whether the High Court or State Government has issued a contrary direction before assuming powers carried over automatically.

sections.title: Withdrawal of powers
sections.raw_text:
(1) The High Court or the State Government, as the case may be, may withdraw all or any of the powers conferred by it under this Sanhita on any person or by any officer subordinate to it.
(2) Any powers conferred by the Chief Judicial Magistrate or by the District Magistrate may be withdrawn by the respective Magistrate by whom such powers were conferred.

breakdown.plain_summary: The power to confer (Section 26) comes with a matching power to withdraw. The High Court or State Government can withdraw powers it granted directly, and also powers granted by any officer subordinate to it — a broad recall authority. Separately, the Chief Judicial Magistrate and District Magistrate each retain the power to withdraw powers they personally conferred.
essential_elements: High Court/State Government may withdraw powers it conferred, or powers conferred by any subordinate officer
Chief Judicial Magistrate may withdraw powers he conferred
District Magistrate may withdraw powers he conferred
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside Section 26 as a conferral/withdrawal pair — the authority that can grant a power generally retains, or is given, a corresponding authority to take it back.

sections.title: Powers of Judges and Magistrates exercisable by their successors-in-office
sections.raw_text:
(1) Subject to the other provisions of this Sanhita, the powers and duties of a Judge or Magistrate may be exercised or performed by his successor-in-office.
(2) When there is any doubt as to who is the successor-in-office, the Sessions Judge shall determine by order in writing the Judge who shall, for the purposes of this Sanhita or of any proceedings or order thereunder, be deemed to be the successor-in-office.
(3) When there is any doubt as to who is the successor-in-office of any Magistrate, the Chief Judicial Magistrate, or the District Magistrate, as the case may be, shall determine by order in writing the Magistrate who shall, for the purpose of this Sanhita or of any proceedings or order thereunder, be deemed to be the successor-in-office of such Magistrate.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section ensures judicial and magisterial business doesn't stall when a Judge or Magistrate leaves office (transfer, retirement, etc.) — the powers and duties simply pass to whoever succeeds them in that office. If it's unclear who that successor actually is, the Sessions Judge resolves the doubt for Judges, and the Chief Judicial Magistrate or District Magistrate resolves it for Magistrates, each by a written order that is deemed conclusive for Sanhita purposes.
essential_elements: A Judge's or Magistrate's powers and duties devolve on his successor-in-office by default
Doubt about who is a Judge's successor: resolved by the Sessions Judge, by written order
Doubt about who is a Magistrate's successor: resolved by the Chief Judicial Magistrate or District Magistrate (as applicable), by written order
exceptions_and_qualifications: This devolution operates “subject to the other provisions of this Sanhita” — more specific rules elsewhere can displace the default succession
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is what allows a pending case or unfinished proceeding to continue seamlessly with a new Judge/Magistrate rather than requiring the entire matter to restart from scratch on every transfer or vacancy.

sections.title: Powers of superior officers of police
sections.raw_text: Police officers superior in rank to an officer in charge of a police station may exercise the same powers, throughout the local area to which they are appointed, as may be exercised by such officer within the limits of his station.
key_terms: officer in charge of a police station

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens the Chapter dealing with police and public duties. It is a simple rank-based power rule: any police officer senior to the officer in charge of a police station automatically holds the same powers as that station officer, but exercisable across the whole local area to which the senior officer is appointed (not just one station's limits) — reflecting the broader territorial charge that typically comes with seniority.
essential_elements: A police officer superior in rank to a station house officer has the same powers as that officer
Exercisable throughout the senior officer's entire appointed local area, not just one station's jurisdiction
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this to confirm that a senior officer (e.g., a Superintendent or Deputy Superintendent) acting outside a specific station's four walls, but within his own charge, is validly exercising powers that formally belong to the station house officer.

sections.title: Public when to assist Magistrates and police
sections.raw_text:
Every person is bound to assist a Magistrate or police officer reasonably demanding his aid—
(a) in the taking or preventing the escape of any other person whom such Magistrate or police officer is authorised to arrest; or
(b) in the prevention or suppression of a breach of the peace; or
(c) in the prevention of any injury attempted to be committed to any public property.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section imposes a legal (not merely moral) duty on every member of the public to help a Magistrate or police officer when reasonably asked, in three specific situations: helping arrest, or stop the escape of, someone the officer is authorised to arrest; helping prevent or stop a breach of the peace; and helping prevent damage being attempted to public property. The demand for aid must be reasonable — this isn't an unlimited conscription power.
essential_elements: Duty applies to every person, when aid is reasonably demanded by a Magistrate or police officer
Covers three situations: assisting a lawful arrest/preventing escape, preventing/suppressing a breach of the peace, and preventing an attempted injury to public property
exceptions_and_qualifications: The demand for assistance must itself be reasonable — an unreasonable demand does not trigger the duty
breakdown.how_to_read: This duty has a penal backstop elsewhere in the substantive criminal law (refusal to assist a public servant is itself punishable) — read this section as defining the scope of the civic duty that such offences are built around.

sections.title: Aid to person, other than police officer, executing warrant
sections.raw_text: When a warrant is directed to a person other than a police officer, any other person may aid in the execution of such warrant, if the person to whom the warrant is directed be near at hand and acting in the execution of the warrant.
key_terms: warrant directed to a private person

breakdown.plain_summary: Warrants aren't always directed to police officers — occasionally the Sanhita allows a warrant to be directed to a private individual. This section allows bystanders to lawfully help that private person execute the warrant, but only if the warrant-holder is himself nearby and actively engaged in executing it — the aid is supplementary to, not a substitute for, the warrant-holder's own presence and action.
essential_elements: Applies only where a warrant is directed to someone other than a police officer
Any other person may aid in its execution
Condition: the person to whom the warrant is directed must be near at hand and actively executing it
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a narrow enabling provision for the relatively unusual case of a private-person warrant — don't confuse it with the general public-duty-to-assist rule in Section 31, which applies to Magistrates and police officers, not private warrant-holders acting alone.

sections.title: Public to give information of certain offences

breakdown.plain_summary: This section imposes an affirmative legal duty on any person who knows about the commission, or planned commission, of a serious listed offence (a long list spanning offences like murder, grievous hurt, offences against the State, kidnapping, and property offences, cross-referenced to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita's numbering) to immediately inform the nearest Magistrate or police officer. The duty extends even to offences that would occur outside India, if the conduct would be an offence had it occurred in India — closing a jurisdictional gap for information about serious extraterritorial criminal activity.
essential_elements: Duty applies to any person aware of the commission, or intended commission, of an offence listed in sub-section (1)'s cross-referenced BNS sections
Information must be given forthwith (immediately) to the nearest Magistrate or police officer
The duty extends to knowledge of acts committed outside India that would be offences if committed in India
exceptions_and_qualifications: Only the specifically enumerated BNS sections trigger this duty — it is not a general duty to report every offence one becomes aware of
breakdown.how_to_read: Keep the enumerated-offences list handy as a checklist — this duty is deliberately narrow and only bites for the serious categories specifically cross-referenced, not for offences generally.

sections.title: Duty of officers employed in connection with affairs of a village to make certain report

breakdown.plain_summary: A rural-specific extension of the public-information duty in Section 33: village officials (panchayat members, headmen, other village-administration functionaries) and indeed every resident of a village must promptly report a defined set of matters to the nearest Magistrate or police station — whichever is closer. The list covers known criminals in the vicinity, non-bailable offences (actual or intended), suspicious or unnatural deaths or disappearances, certain cross-border criminal conduct near the village, and any other matter the District Magistrate specifically directs be reported (with State Government sanction). This provision is especially significant for its coverage of suspicious deaths and disappearances — it functions as an early-warning/first-information mechanism in areas without easy police access.
essential_elements: Duty binds both village officials and ordinary village residents
Report goes to whichever is nearer: the Magistrate or the officer in charge of the nearest police station
Covers six categories: known criminals, non-bailable offences, suspicious deaths/disappearances, certain extraterritorial serious offences, and DM-directed matters

“Village” includes village lands; “proclaimed offender” includes those proclaimed outside Sanhita-extended territory for serious offences; “officer employed in connection with affairs of the village” covers panchayat members, headmen, and village administration officers
exceptions_and_qualifications: The sixth (catch-all) category only applies where the District Magistrate has issued a specific order, itself requiring prior State Government sanction
breakdown.how_to_read: This is functionally a village-level extension of Section 33 — read the two together as the Sanhita's layered information-duty scheme: Section 33 for anyone anywhere regarding serious listed offences, Section 34 for village communities regarding a locally-relevant, broader set of concerns including suspicious deaths.

sections.title: When police may arrest without warrant
sections.raw_text:
(1) Any police officer may without an order from a Magistrate and without a warrant, arrest any person—
(a) who commits, in the presence of a police officer, a cognizable offence; or
(b) against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be less than seven years or which may extend to seven years whether with or without fine, if the following conditions are satisfied, namely:—
(i) the police officer has reason to believe on the basis of such complaint, information, or suspicion that such person has committed the said offence;
(ii) the police officer is satisfied that such arrest is necessary—
(a) to prevent such person from committing any further offence; or
(b) for proper investigation of the offence; or
(c) to prevent such person from causing the evidence of the offence to disappear or tampering with such evidence in any manner; or
(d) to prevent such person from making any inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such facts to the Court or to the police officer; or
(e) as unless such person is arrested, his presence in the Court whenever required cannot be ensured,
and the police officer shall record while making such arrest, his reasons in writing:
Provided that a police officer shall, in all cases where the arrest of a person is not required under the provisions of this sub-section, record the reasons in writing for not making the arrest; or
(c) against whom credible information has been received that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to more than seven years whether with or without fine or with death sentence and the police officer has reason to believe on the basis of that information that such person has committed the said offence; or
(d) who has been proclaimed as an offender either under this Sanhita or by order of the State Government; or
(e) in whose possession anything is found which may reasonably be suspected to be stolen property and who may reasonably be suspected of having committed an offence with reference to such thing; or
(f) who obstructs a police officer while in the execution of his duty, or who has escaped, or attempts to escape, from lawful custody; or
(g) who is reasonably suspected of being a deserter from any of the Armed Forces of the Union; or
(h) who has been concerned in, or against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists, of his having been concerned in, any act committed at any place out of India which, if committed in India, would have been punishable as an offence, and for which he is, under any law relating to extradition, or otherwise, liable to be apprehended or detained in custody in India; or
(i) who, being a released convict, commits a breach of any rule made under sub-section (5) of section 394; or
(j) for whose arrest any requisition, whether written or oral, has been received from another police officer, provided that the requisition specifies the person to be arrested and the offence or other cause for which the arrest is to be made and it appears therefrom that the person might lawfully be arrested without a warrant by the officer who issued the requisition.
(2) Subject to the provisions of section 39, no person concerned in a non-cognizable offence or against whom a complaint has been made or credible information has been received or reasonable suspicion exists of his having so concerned, shall be arrested except under a warrant or order of a Magistrate.
(3) The police officer shall, in all cases where the arrest of a person is not required under sub-section (1) issue a notice directing the person against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence, to appear before him or at such other place as may be specified in the notice.
(4) Where such a notice is issued to any person, it shall be the duty of that person to comply with the terms of the notice.
(5) Where such person complies and continues to comply with the notice, he shall not be arrested in respect of the offence referred to in the notice unless, for reasons to be recorded, the police officer is of the opinion that he ought to be arrested.
(6) Where such person, at any time, fails to comply with the terms of the notice or is unwilling to identify himself, the police officer may, subject to such orders as may have been passed by a competent Court in this behalf, arrest him for the offence mentioned in the notice.
(7) No arrest shall be made without prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police in case of an offence which is punishable for imprisonment of less than three years and such person is infirm or is above sixty years of age.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is one of the most consequential sections in the Sanhita — it defines exactly when police may arrest without going to a Magistrate first. For lower-range cognizable offences (up to 7 years), arrest is not automatic: the officer must additionally satisfy one of five listed necessity grounds (preventing further offences, enabling proper investigation, preventing evidence tampering, preventing witness intimidation, or ensuring court appearance) and must record reasons in writing either way — whether arresting or choosing not to. For the most serious offences (more than 7 years, or death), arrest on credible information plus reason to believe is more straightforward, without the same necessity-ground gate. Where arrest isn't required under sub-section (1), the officer must instead issue a notice compelling appearance — a mechanism carried over and refined from the landmark Arnesh Kumar safeguards, meant to reduce unnecessary arrests for minor cognizable offences. Notice-compliance generally protects against arrest, but non-compliance or refusal to identify oneself can still trigger arrest. Sub-section (7) adds a special protective gate for infirm or elderly (60+) persons accused of minor offences (under 3 years): arrest requires prior clearance from an officer at least Deputy Superintendent of Police rank.
essential_elements: Arrest without warrant permitted for offences committed in an officer's presence, and various listed categories (proclaimed offenders, suspected stolen-property possession, escape from custody, deserters, extraterritorial offences, requisitioned arrests, etc.)

For cognizable offences punishable up to 7 years: arrest requires both reason to believe the person committed the offence AND satisfaction of one of five necessity grounds, with reasons recorded in writing (whether or not arrest is made)
For offences punishable with more than 7 years or death: arrest on credible information and reason to believe, without the necessity-ground gate
Non-cognizable offences: arrest only under a Magistrate's warrant or order (subject to Section 39)
Where arrest isn't required, the officer must issue a notice of appearance; continued compliance generally protects against arrest for that offence
Non-compliance or refusal to identify oneself may lead to arrest, subject to any competent Court's orders
Special safeguard: no arrest of an infirm or 60+-year-old person for an offence punishable under 3 years without prior DSP-rank-or-above permission
exceptions_and_qualifications: The necessity-ground gate under sub-section (1)(b) does not apply to the graver offence category under (1)(c) (more than 7 years/death)
The reasons-in-writing requirement applies symmetrically — both to arrests made and to arrests deliberately not made under sub-section (1)(b)
Sub-section (2)'s Magistrate-warrant requirement for non-cognizable offences is itself subject to Section 39 (arrest on refusal to give name/residence)
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is the statutory codification of the Supreme Court's Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar safeguards — always check first whether the offence falls in the up-to-7-years bracket (triggering the necessity-ground and reasons-in-writing requirements) before assuming arrest is automatic on mere cognizability; then separately check whether the elderly/infirm safeguard in sub-section (7) applies.

sections.title: Procedure of arrest and duties of officer making arrest

breakdown.plain_summary: This section (carried over from the D.K. Basu guidelines, now statutorily codified) sets mandatory procedural safeguards every arresting officer must follow: visible name identification on the officer, a memorandum of arrest witnessed by either a family member of the arrestee or a respectable local resident and countersigned by the arrestee himself, and — unless a family member already witnessed the arrest — informing the arrestee of his right to have someone of his choosing notified of the arrest.
essential_elements: Arresting officer must be clearly, visibly identifiable by name
A memorandum of arrest must be prepared, attested by a family member or respectable local resident, and countersigned by the person arrested
The arrestee must be informed of his right to have a relative, friend, or nominated person told of the arrest, unless a family member already attested the memorandum
breakdown.how_to_read: These are baseline, non-negotiable arrest formalities — treat any arrest lacking a properly witnessed and countersigned memorandum, or lacking the right-to-inform notification, as procedurally defective and worth raising at the earliest opportunity.

sections.title: Designated police officer

breakdown.plain_summary: This section institutionalises transparency around arrests. Every State must run police control rooms at both district and State level, and designate a specific officer (at least Assistant Sub-Inspector rank) in every police station and district responsible for keeping — and prominently displaying, including digitally — up-to-date information on who has been arrested, their addresses, and what offence they're charged with. This makes it easier for families and lawyers to locate a detained person quickly.
essential_elements: Mandatory police control room in every district and at the State level
Designated officer (minimum rank: Assistant Sub-Inspector) in every police station and district responsible for arrest-information records
Information on arrestees' names, addresses and charged offence must be prominently displayed, including digitally
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a locating-and-transparency mechanism, complementing Section 36's right-to-inform — even if an arrestee couldn't immediately notify a relative himself, this section's public/digital display requirement gives another route for family or counsel to find them.

sections.title: Right of arrested person to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation
sections.raw_text: When any person is arrested and interrogated by the police, he shall be entitled to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout interrogation.

breakdown.plain_summary: A newly codified right for arrested persons: they may meet an advocate of their own choosing during the interrogation process. The right is real but limited — it is a right to meet counsel during interrogation, not a right to have the advocate physically present throughout the entire interrogation session.
essential_elements: Applies to any person arrested and interrogated by the police
Entitled to meet an advocate of his own choice during the interrogation
exceptions_and_qualifications: The right is to meet counsel during interrogation, not to have the advocate present throughout the whole interrogation
breakdown.how_to_read: Note this deliberate limitation carefully — the section grants a meeting right, which is narrower than a continuous-presence right; don't overstate its scope when advising a client or arguing a procedural violation.

sections.title: Arrest on refusal to give name and residence
sections.raw_text:
(1) When any person who, in the presence of a police officer, has committed or has been accused of committing a non-cognizable offence refuses on demand of such officer to give his name and residence or gives a name or residence which such officer has reason to believe to be false, he may be arrested by such officer in order that his name or residence may be ascertained.
(2) When the true name and residence of such person have been ascertained, he shall be released on a bond or bail bond, to appear before a Magistrate if so required:
Provided that if such person is not resident in India, the bail bond shall be secured by a surety or sureties resident in India.
(3) If the true name and residence of such person is not ascertained within twenty-four hours from the time of arrest or if he fails to execute the bond or bail bond, or, if so required, to furnish sufficient sureties, he shall forthwith be forwarded to the nearest Magistrate having jurisdiction.
key_terms: refusal to give name and residence

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a narrow exception to the general rule (Section 35(2)) that non-cognizable offences require a warrant for arrest: if someone commits or is accused of a non-cognizable offence in an officer's presence and then refuses to give (or lies about) their name and residence, the officer may arrest them purely to establish identity — not to punish the underlying offence. Once identity is verified, the person must be released on a bond/bail bond (with an India-resident surety required if the person isn't India-resident) to appear before a Magistrate if needed. If identity still can't be confirmed within 24 hours, or bond/surety conditions aren't met, the person must be produced before the nearest Magistrate.
essential_elements: Applies only to non-cognizable offences committed or accused in the officer's presence
Triggered by refusal to give name/residence, or giving information the officer believes to be false
Arrest is for the limited purpose of ascertaining identity, not investigating the offence itself
Once identity is confirmed: release on bond/bail bond (non-residents require an India-resident surety)
24-hour outer limit: if identity remains unascertained, or bond/surety isn't furnished, produce before the nearest Magistrate
breakdown.how_to_read: This provision is entirely about identity verification, not offence investigation — the moment true name and residence are established, the default outcome is release on bond, not continued detention.

sections.title: Arrest by private person and procedure on such arrest
sections.raw_text:
(1) Any private person may arrest or cause to be arrested any person who in his presence commits a non-bailable and cognizable offence, or any proclaimed offender, and, without unnecessary delay, but within six hours from such arrest, shall make over or cause to be made over any person so arrested to a police officer, or, in the absence of a police officer, take such person or cause him to be taken in custody to the nearest police station.
(2) If there is reason to believe that such person comes under the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 35, a police officer shall take him in custody.
(3) If there is reason to believe that he has committed a non-cognizable offence, and he refuses on the demand of a police officer to give his name and residence, or gives a name or residence which such officer has reason to believe to be false, he shall be dealt with under the provisions of section 39; but if there is no sufficient reason to believe that he has committed any offence, he shall be at once released.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the “citizen's arrest” power: any private person may personally arrest someone who commits a non-bailable and cognizable offence in their presence, or a proclaimed offender, but this power comes with a strict, new time limit — the arrested person must be handed to police, or taken to the nearest station, within six hours (without unnecessary delay). Once handed over, the police officer's response depends on the facts: full custody if Section 35(1)'s arrest-without-warrant grounds are met, the name/residence-verification route under Section 39 if it's a non-cognizable offence with an identity refusal, or immediate release if there's no sufficient reason to believe any offence was committed at all.
essential_elements: Private persons may arrest anyone committing a non-bailable and cognizable offence in their presence, or a proclaimed offender
Must hand over to police (or take to nearest station) without unnecessary delay, and in any case within six hours

Police then decide the person's fate: full custody (if Section 35(1) grounds apply), Section 39 identity-verification route (if non-cognizable offence with identity refusal), or immediate release (if no sufficient reason to believe an offence occurred)
exceptions_and_qualifications: The six-hour outer limit is a new, more specific safeguard than the old CrPC's vaguer “without unnecessary delay” standard alone
breakdown.how_to_read: The six-hour cap is the standout feature versus the old law — always check the timeline between a private arrest and handover to police, since exceeding six hours is now a specific, checkable procedural lapse.

sections.title: Arrest by Magistrate
sections.raw_text:
(1) When any offence is committed in the presence of a Magistrate, whether Executive or Judicial, within his local jurisdiction, he may himself arrest or order any person to arrest the offender, and may thereupon, subject to the provisions herein contained as to bail, commit the offender to custody.
(2) Any Magistrate, whether Executive or Judicial, may at any time arrest or direct the arrest, in his presence, within his local jurisdiction, of any person for whose arrest he is competent at the time and in the circumstances to issue a warrant.

breakdown.plain_summary: Magistrates (whether Executive or Judicial) have their own direct arrest power within their local jurisdiction. If an offence occurs right in front of a Magistrate, he may personally arrest the offender, or order someone else to do so, and commit the offender to custody, subject to the Sanhita's bail provisions. More broadly, a Magistrate may also arrest, or order the arrest of, anyone present before him for whom he could — at that time, under those circumstances — lawfully issue an arrest warrant, without needing to formally issue that warrant first.
essential_elements: Offence committed in a Magistrate's presence, within his local jurisdiction: he may personally arrest, or order arrest, and commit to custody (subject to bail provisions)
Broader power: a Magistrate may arrest, or direct arrest, of any person in his presence for whom he could lawfully issue a warrant at that time
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a direct, on-the-spot judicial arrest power, distinct from the police's Section 35 power — note it applies to both Executive and Judicial Magistrates, and the second limb is broader than the first since it doesn't require the offence itself to occur in the Magistrate's presence, only the person to be present when the Magistrate could otherwise have issued a warrant.

sections.title: Protection of members of Armed Forces from arrest
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in section 35 and sections 39 to 41 (both inclusive), no member of the Armed Forces of the Union shall be arrested for anything done or purported to be done by him in the discharge of his official duties except after obtaining the consent of the Central Government.
(2) The State Government may, by notification, direct that the provisions of sub-section (1) shall apply to such class or category of the members of the Force charged with the maintenance of public order as may be specified therein, wherever they may be serving, and thereupon the provisions of that sub-section shall apply as if for the expression “Central Government” occurring therein, the expression “State Government” were substituted.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a protective, non-obstante shield for Armed Forces personnel: notwithstanding the general arrest powers in Sections 35 and 39-41, no member of the Armed Forces of the Union can be arrested for acts done, or purportedly done, in discharge of official duty without prior Central Government consent. Sub-section (2) allows the State Government to extend an equivalent protection (with State Government consent substituted for Central) to specified categories of public-order forces under its own control, wherever they serve.
essential_elements: No arrest of an Armed Forces of the Union member for acts done/purported to be done in official duty, without prior Central Government consent
Overrides Sections 35 and 39-41 to that extent
State Government may extend an equivalent protection (with State Government consent) to specified public-order force categories under its control
exceptions_and_qualifications: The protection covers only acts done, or purported to be done, in discharge of official duties — it is not a blanket immunity from arrest for any conduct
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a narrow immunity tied strictly to official-duty conduct — always separate out whether the alleged act was genuinely connected to official duty before assuming this protection applies.

sections.title: Arrest how made
sections.raw_text:
(1) In making an arrest the police officer or other person making the same shall actually touch or confine the body of the person to be arrested, unless there be a submission to the custody by word or action:
Provided that where a woman is to be arrested, unless the circumstances indicate to the contrary, her submission to custody on an oral intimation of arrest shall be presumed and, unless the circumstances otherwise require or unless the police officer is a female, the police officer shall not touch the person of the woman for making her arrest.
(2) If such person forcibly resists the endeavour to arrest him, or attempts to evade the arrest, such police officer or other person may use all means necessary to effect the arrest.
(3) The police officer may, keeping in view the nature and gravity of the offence, use handcuff while making the arrest of a person or while producing such person before the court who is a habitual or repeat offender, or who escaped from custody, or who has committed offence of organised crime, terrorist act, drug related crime, or illegal possession of arms and ammunition, murder, rape, acid attack, counterfeiting of coins and currency-notes, human trafficking, sexual offence against children, or offence against the State.
(4) Nothing in this section gives a right to cause the death of a person who is not accused of an offence punishable with death or with imprisonment for life.
(5) Save in exceptional circumstances, no woman shall be arrested after sunset and before sunrise, and where such exceptional circumstances exist, the woman police officer shall, by making a written report, obtain the prior permission of the Magistrate of the first class within whose local jurisdiction the offence is committed or the arrest is to be made.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section prescribes the physical mechanics of a lawful arrest and its limits. The default method is actual physical touch/confinement, unless the person submits by word or conduct — with a special, gender-sensitive rule for women: submission is presumed on a mere oral statement of arrest, and a male officer generally may not touch her to effect the arrest. Force may be used, but only as necessary, if the person forcibly resists or tries to evade arrest. Handcuffs are conditionally permitted — a significant new, explicit statutory basis — but only calibrated to the offence's nature/gravity and limited to specific serious categories (habitual/repeat offenders, escapees, organised crime, terrorism, drug offences, illegal arms possession, murder, rape, acid attacks, counterfeiting, human trafficking, child sexual offences, offences against the State). Deadly force is never authorised unless the person is accused of a death- or life-imprisonment-punishable offence. And women generally cannot be arrested at night (after sunset, before sunrise), except in exceptional circumstances requiring prior written permission from a first-class Magistrate.
essential_elements: Arrest is made by actual touch/confinement, unless the person submits by word or action
Special rule for women: oral intimation is presumed to secure submission; male officers generally may not touch a woman to arrest her
Necessary force may be used against forcible resistance or attempted evasion
Handcuffs may be used, calibrated to offence nature/gravity, only for specifically listed serious offence categories or repeat/escaped offenders
No right to cause death unless the person is accused of an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment
No arrest of a woman between sunset and sunrise except in exceptional circumstances, requiring prior written first-class-Magistrate permission obtained by a woman police officer
exceptions_and_qualifications: The no-touch rule for women yields where circumstances indicate otherwise, or where the arresting officer is herself female
The night-arrest-of-women bar yields only in exceptional circumstances, and even then requires prior Magisterial permission obtained in writing
breakdown.how_to_read: Note that sub-section (3)'s handcuffing power is a genuinely new statutory feature (the old CrPC had no explicit handcuffing provision, and courts had restricted routine handcuffing) — always check whether the offence falls within the specifically enumerated categories before treating handcuffing as lawful.

sections.title: Search of place entered by person sought to be arrested
sections.raw_text:
(1) If any person acting under a warrant of arrest, or any police officer having authority to arrest, has reason to believe that the person to be arrested has entered into, or is within, any place, any person residing in, or being in charge of, such place shall, on demand of such person acting as aforesaid or such police officer, allow him free ingress thereto, and afford all reasonable facilities for a search therein.
(2) If ingress to such place cannot be obtained under sub-section (1), it shall be lawful in any case for a person acting under a warrant and in any case in which a warrant may issue, but cannot be obtained without affording the person to be arrested an opportunity of escape, for a police officer to enter such place and search therein, and in order to effect an entrance into such place, to break open any outer or inner door or window of any house or place, whether that of the person to be arrested or of any other person, if after notification of his authority and purpose, and demand of admittance duly made, he cannot otherwise obtain admittance:
Provided that if any such place is an apartment in the actual occupancy of a female (not being the person to be arrested) who, according to custom, does not appear in public, such person or police officer shall, before entering such apartment, give notice to such female that she is at liberty to withdraw and shall afford her every reasonable facility for withdrawing, and may then break open the apartment and enter it.
(3) Any police officer or other person authorised to make an arrest may break open any outer or inner door or window of any house or place in order to liberate himself or any other person who, having lawfully entered for the purpose of making an arrest, is detained therein.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section gives arresting authorities a right of entry to search premises where the person sought is believed to be. The occupier/person-in-charge must first be given the chance to allow free entry voluntarily. Only if that voluntary entry is refused (or entry would let the person escape) can the officer forcibly break open doors/windows — but only after first announcing authority and purpose and demanding admittance. A specific cultural/privacy safeguard applies to a female occupant (not the person being arrested) who observes purdah (customary seclusion): she must first be notified and given a reasonable chance to withdraw before her apartment is forced open. Finally, if an authorised arresting person is himself trapped or detained inside after lawfully entering, he may break open doors/windows to free himself or another such person.
essential_elements: Occupier/person-in-charge must first be asked to allow free entry and afford reasonable search facilities
Forcible entry (breaking open doors/windows) permitted only after announcement of authority/purpose and demand of admittance goes unmet, or where waiting would let the person escape
Purdah safeguard: a female occupant not being the person sought must be notified and allowed to withdraw before her apartment is forced open
Self-liberation right: an arresting person lawfully inside but detained may break open doors/windows to free himself or another
exceptions_and_qualifications: The purdah safeguard's notice-and-withdrawal step is mandatory before entry into that specific apartment, even once forcible entry to the premises generally is otherwise justified
breakdown.how_to_read: Always check the sequencing here — announcement and a genuine demand for admittance must precede any forced entry, and the purdah-related notice/withdrawal opportunity is an additional, separate step specifically for the described category of female occupant before her particular apartment is breached.

sections.title: Pursuit of offenders into other jurisdictions
sections.raw_text: A police officer may, for the purpose of arresting without warrant any person whom he is authorised to arrest, pursue such person into any place in India.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section removes territorial jurisdiction as a barrier when a police officer is chasing someone he is already authorised to arrest without a warrant — he may follow that person into any place in India, regardless of whether it falls outside his own local jurisdiction. This is the statutory basis for “hot pursuit” across jurisdictional boundaries.
essential_elements: Applies only where the officer is already authorised to make a warrantless arrest of the person
Permits pursuit into any place in India, without territorial limitation
breakdown.how_to_read: This section only authorises pursuit, not an independent arrest power — the officer's underlying authority to arrest without warrant must already exist (typically under Section 35) before this cross-jurisdictional pursuit right comes into play.

sections.title: No unnecessary restraint
sections.raw_text: The person arrested shall not be subjected to more restraint than is necessary to prevent his escape.

breakdown.plain_summary: A one-line but important safeguard: once a person is arrested, the police may restrain them only to the extent needed to stop them from escaping — nothing more. Excess force or restraint beyond what escape-prevention requires is unlawful, even against a validly arrested person.
essential_elements: Applies to any person arrested (regardless of the arrest's legal basis).
Restraint permitted only 'to prevent his escape' — that is the sole justification.
Any restraint beyond this necessity threshold is impermissible.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a general principle, not a specific procedure — its practical content is filled in by later provisions (e.g., Section 43's rules on handcuffing) and by constitutional/human-rights jurisprudence on custodial treatment.
breakdown.how_to_read: A short but frequently pleaded provision in custodial-torture or excessive-force complaints — cite it alongside Section 43(3)'s handcuffing restrictions and Article 21 case law when restraint clearly exceeded escape-prevention.

sections.title: Person arrested to be informed of grounds of arrest and of right to bail
sections.raw_text:
(1) Every police officer or other person arresting any person without warrant shall forthwith communicate to him full particulars of the offence for which he is arrested or other grounds for such arrest.
(2) Where a police officer arrests without warrant any person other than a person accused of a non-bailable offence, he shall inform the person arrested that he is entitled to be released on bail and that he may arrange for sureties on his behalf.

breakdown.plain_summary: Two distinct duties on the arresting officer, both immediate ('forthwith'): first, always tell the person exactly why they are being arrested — the specific offence or grounds, not a vague label. Second, if the offence is bailable, also tell them they have a right to bail and may arrange sureties. This second duty does not apply to non-bailable offences (where bail isn't a matter of right).
essential_elements: Sub-section (1) applies to every warrantless arrest, for any offence — full particulars of the offence/grounds must be communicated immediately.
Sub-section (2) applies only where the offence is NOT non-bailable — the arrested person must additionally be told of the bail right and the option to arrange sureties.
Both duties fall on 'every police officer or other person' making the arrest — including private persons making a citizen's arrest under Section 40.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The right to be told of the bail option is expressly carved out for non-bailable offences — no such disclosure duty arises there, since bail is discretionary, not automatic.
breakdown.how_to_read: Failure to communicate grounds of arrest is a well-established ground for challenging the legality of custody (habeas corpus/Article 22 territory) — this section is the statutory backbone for that constitutional guarantee. Always check the arrest memo/case diary for a contemporaneous record of this communication.

sections.title: Obligation of person making arrest to inform about arrest, etc., to relative or friend
sections.raw_text:
(1) Every police officer or other person making any arrest under this Sanhita shall forthwith give the information regarding such arrest and place where the arrested person is being held to any of his relatives, friends or such other persons as may be disclosed or nominated by the arrested person for the purpose of giving such information and also to the designated police officer in the district.
(2) The police officer shall inform the arrested person of his rights under sub-section (1) as soon as he is brought to the police station.
(3) An entry of the fact as to who has been informed of the arrest of such person shall be made in a book to be kept in the police station in such form as the State Government may, by rules, provide.
(4) It shall be the duty of the Magistrate before whom such arrested person is produced, to satisfy himself that the requirements of sub-section (2) and sub-section (3) have been complied with in respect of such arrested person.

breakdown.plain_summary: This codifies the D.K. Basu right-to-inform safeguard: someone nominated by the arrested person (and the district's designated police officer under Section 37) must be told immediately of the arrest and where the person is being held. The person must be told of this right as soon as they reach the station, the disclosure must be logged in a register, and the Magistrate before whom they are produced must actively verify these steps were followed — not just take it on trust.
essential_elements: Information goes to whoever the arrested person discloses/nominates (relative, friend, or other), plus the designated police officer in the district.
The arrested person must be informed of this right as soon as they are brought to the station.
A register entry recording who was informed is mandatory.
The Magistrate has an affirmative duty to satisfy themselves that sub-sections (2) and (3) were complied with — this is a judicial check, not just a police obligation.
exceptions_and_qualifications: No express exception in the text — the duty is unconditional once an arrest under the Sanhita is made.
breakdown.how_to_read: Magistrates should be pressed at first production to record on file that they specifically verified compliance with sub-sections (2)-(3); defence counsel should demand the station register entry as documentary proof where custodial notification is disputed.

sections.title: Search of arrested person
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whenever—
(i) a person is arrested by a police officer under a warrant which does not provide for the taking of bail, or under a warrant which provides for the taking of bail but the person arrested cannot furnish bail; and
(ii) a person is arrested without warrant, or by a private person under a warrant, and cannot legally be admitted to bail, or is unable to furnish bail, the officer making the arrest or, when the arrest is made by a private person, the police officer to whom he makes over the person arrested, may search such person, and place in safe custody all articles, other than necessary wearing-apparel, found upon him and where any article is seized from the arrested person, a receipt showing the articles taken in possession by the police officer shall be given to such person.
(2) Whenever it is necessary to cause a female to be searched, the search shall be made by another female with strict regard to decency.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once a person cannot be released on bail (either because the warrant blocks it or they simply can't furnish it), the arresting officer may search them and take all their belongings into safe custody — except the clothes they need to wear. Anything seized must be receipted. A woman being searched must be searched only by another woman, with strict regard to decency.
essential_elements: Search power is conditional on the person NOT being released on bail — either warrant-blocked or unable to furnish bail.
Only non-wearing-apparel articles may be seized and held in safe custody.
A receipt must be given for any article seized.
Female searches must be conducted by a female officer/person, with strict decency.
exceptions_and_qualifications: If the person is admitted to bail, this search-and-seizure power under this section does not apply.
breakdown.how_to_read: Insist on the seizure receipt in every case — its absence is a common and effective challenge to the integrity of the property/recovery trail in a later trial. The female-search safeguard is non-negotiable and its breach independently taints the search.

sections.title: Power to seize offensive weapons
sections.raw_text: The police officer or other person making any arrest under this Sanhita may, immediately after the arrest is made, take from the person arrested any offensive weapons which he has about his person, and shall deliver all weapons so taken to the Court or officer before which or whom the officer or person making the arrest is required by this Sanhita to produce the person arrested.

breakdown.plain_summary: Immediately upon arrest, any weapons found on the person may be seized — and must then be handed over to whichever Court or officer the arrested person is required to be produced before. This is a mandatory chain-of-custody step, not discretionary once weapons are found.
essential_elements: Seizure is permitted 'immediately after the arrest is made.'
Applies to 'offensive weapons' found on the person.
Weapons seized MUST be delivered to the Court/officer before whom the arrested person is to be produced — this part is mandatory ('shall').
breakdown.how_to_read: A clean weapon-seizure and hand-over trail (seizure memo, delivery record to the producing Court/officer) is often decisive in weapon-related offences — gaps here are a standard defence attack point.

sections.title: Examination of accused by medical practitioner at request of police officer
sections.raw_text:
(1) When a person is arrested on a charge of committing an offence of such a nature and alleged to have been committed under such circumstances that there are reasonable grounds for believing that an examination of his person will afford evidence as to the commission of an offence, it shall be lawful for a registered medical practitioner, acting at the request of any police officer, and for any person acting in good faith in his aid and under his direction, to make such an examination of the person arrested as is reasonably necessary in order to ascertain the facts which may afford such evidence, and to use such force as is reasonably necessary for that purpose.
(2) Whenever the person of a female is to be examined under this section, the examination shall be made only by, or under the supervision of, a female registered medical practitioner.
(3) The registered medical practitioner shall, without any delay, forward the examination report to the investigating officer.
Explanation.—In this section and sections 52 and 53,—
(a) "examination" shall include the examination of blood, blood stains, semen, swabs in case of sexual offences, sputum and sweat, hair samples and finger nail clippings by the use of modern and scientific techniques including DNA profiling and such other tests which the registered medical practitioner thinks necessary in a particular case;
(b) "registered medical practitioner" means a medical practitioner who possesses any medical qualification recognised under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019 (30 of 2019) and whose name has been entered in the National Medical Register or a State Medical Register under that Act.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where the circumstances of the alleged offence make it likely that a medical examination of the accused's body will yield evidence, a registered doctor may examine the arrested person at police request — using reasonable force if needed. 'Examination' expressly covers modern forensic techniques including DNA profiling. If the accused is female, only a female doctor (or examination under her supervision) is permitted. The report must go promptly to the investigating officer.
essential_elements: Threshold: 'reasonable grounds for believing' the examination will afford evidence of the offence — not a mere fishing expedition.
Only a registered medical practitioner (or someone acting in good faith under their direction) may conduct it.
Reasonable force may be used to carry out the examination.
Female accused persons must be examined only by, or under supervision of, a female registered medical practitioner.
'Examination' is defined broadly to include DNA profiling and other modern scientific techniques.
Report must be forwarded to the investigating officer without delay.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'reasonable force' power is itself bounded by reasonableness — it is not unlimited force.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the general medical-examination-of-accused power (distinct from Section 52's rape-specific procedure and Section 53's arrival medical check) — useful wherever bodily evidence (injuries, bite marks, biological trace evidence) is relevant to proving the offence, not just in sexual-offence cases.

sections.title: Examination of person accused of rape by medical practitioner

breakdown.plain_summary: A specialised version of Section 51 for rape/attempted-rape accusations: the examining doctor should ordinarily be a government/local-authority hospital doctor, with a private registered practitioner as fallback only if none is available within 16 km. The report is far more detailed than the general Section 51 report — name/address, age, injury marks, DNA-profiling material description, and reasoned conclusions with exact examination timing — and it must be routed through the investigating officer to the Magistrate as part of the Section 193 chargesheet documents.
essential_elements: Applies specifically to persons arrested on a charge of rape or attempt to commit rape.
Preferred examiner: a registered medical practitioner employed at a government/local-authority hospital.
Fallback to any other registered medical practitioner only if no such government-employed practitioner is within 16 km of the offence location.
The report must contain the five specified particulars, precise reasons for each conclusion, and exact start/end times.
The report must ultimately reach the Magistrate under Section 193 as part of the investigation documents.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 16-kilometre proximity rule is the sole trigger for using a non-government practitioner — it is a geographic, not a convenience-based, exception.
breakdown.how_to_read: Defence counsel routinely scrutinise this report for compliance with the mandatory particulars and timing — a report missing DNA-material description or exact examination times is vulnerable to challenge on reliability grounds. Prosecutors should ensure the chain to Section 193 documents is unbroken.

sections.title: Examination of arrested person by medical officer
sections.raw_text:
(1) When any person is arrested, he shall be examined by a medical officer in the service of the Central Government or a State Government, and in case the medical officer is not available, by a registered medical practitioner soon after the arrest is made:
Provided that if the medical officer or the registered medical practitioner is of the opinion that one more examination of such person is necessary, he may do so:
Provided further that where the arrested person is a female, the examination of the body shall be made only by or under the supervision of a female medical officer, and in case the female medical officer is not available, by a female registered medical practitioner.
(2) The medical officer or a registered medical practitioner so examining the arrested person shall prepare the record of such examination, mentioning therein any injuries or marks of violence upon the person arrested, and the approximate time when such injuries or marks may have been inflicted.
(3) Where an examination is made under sub-section (1), a copy of the report of such examination shall be furnished by the medical officer or registered medical practitioner, as the case may be, to the arrested person or the person nominated by such arrested person.

breakdown.plain_summary: Unlike Sections 51-52 (which are evidence-gathering examinations requested by police for a specific offence), this is a baseline, mandatory arrival check for every arrested person, meant to document their physical condition at the point of custody — a key safeguard against later custodial abuse. Government medical officers are examiners of first choice, with private registered practitioners as fallback, and female arrestees must be examined by/under a female practitioner. A copy of the report goes to the arrested person or their nominee — giving them documentary proof of their condition on entering custody.
essential_elements: Applies to every arrested person, without any offence-specific trigger — this is a general, mandatory custodial-entry examination.
Primary examiner: a government (Central or State) medical officer; registered medical practitioner as fallback if unavailable.
A further examination may be conducted if the examining practitioner considers it necessary.
Female arrestees: examination only by, or under supervision of, a female medical officer/practitioner.
The record must note injuries or marks of violence and their approximate time of infliction.
A copy of the report must be given to the arrested person or their nominee.
breakdown.how_to_read: This report, taken at the point of arrest, is the single most important documentary defence against later custodial-violence allegations against police — always obtain and preserve the copy given under sub-section (3); its absence or a mismatch with a later medical report is strong evidence of custodial mistreatment.

sections.title: Identification of person arrested
sections.raw_text:
Where a person is arrested on a charge of committing an offence and his identification by any other person or persons is considered necessary for the purpose of investigation of such offence, the Court, having jurisdiction may, on the request of the officer in charge of a police station, direct the person so arrested to subject himself to identification by any person or persons in such manner as the Court may deem fit:
Provided that if the person identifying the person arrested is mentally or physically disabled, such process of identification shall take place under the supervision of a Magistrate who shall take appropriate steps to ensure that such person identifies the person arrested using methods that person is comfortable with and the identification process shall be recorded by any audio-video electronic means.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the statutory basis for what is commonly called a Test Identification Parade (TIP) — the Court, on the police's request, may direct the arrested person to be identified by witnesses. Where the identifying witness has a mental or physical disability, the process gets extra judicial protection: it must be Magistrate-supervised, adapted to methods the witness is comfortable with, and video-recorded.
essential_elements: Trigger: identification by another person/persons is 'considered necessary' for the investigation.
Only the Court (having jurisdiction), acting on the police's request, can direct the identification.
The manner of identification is left to the Court's discretion, subject to the proviso.
Where the identifying witness is mentally or physically disabled: Magistrate supervision, comfortable methods, and mandatory audio-video recording.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The disabled-witness safeguards in the proviso are additional procedural protections, not a bar on holding the identification at all.
breakdown.how_to_read: A properly conducted TIP under this section (with fair line-up composition and, where relevant, video recording) substantially strengthens an identification-based prosecution case; a TIP conducted in violation of the proviso's safeguards for a disabled witness is a ready ground of challenge to that evidence's reliability.

sections.title: Procedure when police officer deputes subordinate to arrest without warrant
sections.raw_text:
(1) When any officer in charge of a police station or any police officer making an investigation under Chapter XIII requires any officer subordinate to him to arrest without a warrant (otherwise than in his presence) any person who may lawfully be arrested without a warrant, he shall deliver to the officer required to make the arrest an order in writing, specifying the person to be arrested and the offence or other cause for which the arrest is to be made and the officer so required shall, before making the arrest, notify to the person to be arrested the substance of the order and, if so required by such person, shall show him the order.
(2) Nothing in sub-section (1) shall affect the power of a police officer to arrest a person under section 35.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a senior police officer wants a subordinate to make a warrantless arrest without the senior being physically present, the delegation must be documented: a written order naming the person to be arrested and the offence/cause, which the subordinate must disclose (and show, if asked) to the person before arresting them. This does not cut down the ordinary Section 35 power to arrest without warrant on the spot.
essential_elements: Applies only when the deputing officer will NOT be present at the arrest.
A written order specifying the person and the offence/cause is mandatory.
The subordinate officer must notify the substance of the order to the person before arrest, and show the written order itself if the person asks.
Sub-section (2) preserves the independent Section 35 arrest power untouched.
breakdown.how_to_read: Where an arrest is challenged as an improper delegation, demand production of the written order under sub-section (1) — its absence, when the deputing officer was admittedly not present, is a clean procedural defect.

sections.title: Health and safety of arrested person
sections.raw_text: It shall be the duty of the person having the custody of an accused to take reasonable care of the health and safety of the accused.

breakdown.plain_summary: A general, continuing duty on whoever holds an arrested/accused person in custody — not just at the moment of arrest, but throughout custody — to take reasonable care of their health and safety.
essential_elements: Duty-holder: 'the person having the custody' — covers police custody as well as any other custodial arrangement under the Sanhita.
Standard is 'reasonable care,' a continuing obligation, not a one-time check.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Section 53's arrival medical check — Section 53 documents the baseline condition, Section 56 is the ongoing duty that makes any deterioration in that condition during custody legally significant.

sections.title: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station
sections.raw_text: A police officer making an arrest without warrant shall, without unnecessary delay and subject to the provisions herein contained as to bail, take or send the person arrested before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police station.

breakdown.plain_summary: After a warrantless arrest, the police must produce the person before a Magistrate with jurisdiction, or before the station house officer, without unnecessary delay — this is the procedural gateway into the 24-hour production requirement of Section 58 and Article 22 of the Constitution.
essential_elements: Applies to warrantless arrests.
Standard: 'without unnecessary delay' — not a fixed number of hours by itself (that comes from Section 58), but delay must be justified by circumstance.
Production is either before a jurisdictional Magistrate or the officer in charge of a police station.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Subject to bail provisions — if the person is released on bail before production becomes due, this obligation is correspondingly affected.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Sections 57 and 58 together as a single production-and-time-limit safeguard — an unexplained gap between arrest and production, even within the 24-hour outer limit, can still be challenged as 'unnecessary delay' under this section.

sections.title: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours
sections.raw_text: No police officer shall detain in custody a person arrested without warrant for a longer period than under all the circumstances of the case is reasonable, and such period shall not, in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under section 187, exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court, whether having jurisdiction or not.

breakdown.plain_summary: The constitutional 24-hour rule in statutory form: police custody without a Magistrate's order cannot exceed 24 hours, and travel time to the Magistrate's Court doesn't count against that limit. Only a special order of a Magistrate under Section 187 (police custody/remand) can extend detention beyond 24 hours.
essential_elements: Outer limit: 24 hours of police custody without judicial authorisation.
Travel time from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court is excluded from the 24-hour count.
Extension beyond 24 hours requires a special order of a Magistrate under Section 187.
The 'reasonable under the circumstances' standard applies even within the 24-hour ceiling — the ceiling is a maximum, not an entitlement to use the full time.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the single most litigated custodial-timeline provision — always calculate the exact arrest time versus production time, and cross-check whether any journey-time exclusion is genuinely justified rather than a pretext for extended interrogation.

sections.title: Police to report apprehensions
sections.raw_text: Officers in charge of police stations shall report to the District Magistrate, or, if he so directs, to the Sub-divisional Magistrate, the cases of all persons arrested without warrant, within the limits of their respective stations, whether such persons have been admitted to bail or otherwise.

breakdown.plain_summary: A supervisory/oversight reporting duty: station house officers must report every warrantless-arrest case within their jurisdiction to the District Magistrate (or the Sub-divisional Magistrate, if the DM so directs) — regardless of whether the arrested person was granted bail.
essential_elements: Applies to all warrantless arrests within the station's territorial limits.
Reporting is to the District Magistrate by default, or the Sub-divisional Magistrate if the DM directs reporting there instead.
Bail status of the arrested person is irrelevant to the reporting duty — both bailed and non-bailed cases must be reported.
breakdown.how_to_read: A useful oversight mechanism to invoke in cases of suspected mass or arbitrary arrests — the DM/SDM reporting trail can be sought via RTI or court direction to establish patterns of police conduct in a locality.

sections.title: Discharge of person apprehended
sections.raw_text: No person who has been arrested by a police officer shall be discharged except on his bond, or bail bond, or under the special order of a Magistrate.

breakdown.plain_summary: An arrested person cannot simply be let go informally — release must happen through one of three defined channels: execution of a bond, execution of a bail bond, or a Magistrate's special order.
essential_elements: Applies to release/discharge of any person arrested by a police officer.
Only three valid discharge routes: bond, bail bond, or special Magistrate's order.
breakdown.how_to_read: If a person is released without any of these three formalities being completed (or re-arrested despite one being in place), that irregularity itself can be raised as a procedural defect.

sections.title: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake
sections.raw_text:
(1) If a person in lawful custody escapes or is rescued, the person from whose custody he escaped or was rescued may immediately pursue and arrest him in any place in India.
(2) The provisions of section 44 shall apply to arrests under sub-section (1) although the person making any such arrest is not acting under a warrant and is not a police officer having authority to arrest.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a lawfully-held person escapes (or is rescued by others), whoever had custody of them may chase and re-arrest them anywhere in India, without needing a fresh warrant. Section 44's rules on entering premises to make an arrest apply equally here, even though the pursuer may not otherwise be a police officer with arrest authority.
essential_elements: Trigger: escape from, or rescue out of, lawful custody.
The pursuer is the person from whose custody the escape/rescue occurred.
Pursuit and re-arrest are permitted anywhere in India — no territorial limit.
Section 44's search-of-premises procedure applies to this pursuit-arrest even for a non-police pursuer.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section, read with Section 45 (hot pursuit across jurisdictions for ordinary arrests), completes the Sanhita's cross-jurisdictional pursuit scheme — useful when custody-escape cases raise territorial-jurisdiction objections to the re-arrest.

sections.title: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita
sections.raw_text: No arrest shall be made except in accordance with the provisions of this Sanhita or any other law for the time being in force providing for arrest.

breakdown.plain_summary: The closing provision of the Arrest of Persons chapter: a blanket rule that every arrest must conform either to the Sanhita's own procedure or to whatever other specific law authorises the arrest in question (e.g., special/local statutes).
