It is the statutory anchor for arguing that any deviation from the prescribed arrest procedure renders the arrest itself unlawful.
essential_elements: Applies to all arrests, under the Sanhita or under any other law currently in force that provides for arrest.
Compliance must be 'strictly according to' the applicable provisions — not merely substantial or good-faith compliance.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the natural closing citation for any arrest-procedure challenge — after establishing which specific safeguard (Sections 35-61) was breached, cite Section 62 to argue the breach renders the whole arrest non-compliant with the Sanhita, not just a technical slip.

sections.title: Form of summons
sections.raw_text:
Every summons issued by a Court under this Sanhita shall be—
(i) in writing, in duplicate, signed by the presiding officer of such Court or by such other officer as the High Court may, from time to time, by rule direct, and shall bear the seal of the Court; or
(ii) in an encrypted or any other form of electronic communication and shall bear the image of the seal of the Court or digital signature.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Chapter VI's scheme for compelling a person's appearance before Court. Every summons must be in writing, made in duplicate, and signed by the presiding officer (or a High-Court-authorised officer), bearing the Court's seal — a genuinely new BNSS feature is that a summons can now equally be issued electronically, bearing an image of the seal or a digital signature, formally recognising e-summons as valid.
essential_elements: Two valid forms: (i) written, duplicate, signed, sealed paper summons, or (ii) encrypted/electronic summons bearing the seal's image or a digital signature.
Must be signed by the presiding officer, or an officer the High Court has authorised by rule.
breakdown.how_to_read: The explicit electronic-summons option is a significant procedural modernisation over the old CrPC — practitioners should check the applicable High Court rules on the manner/form of digital signature and electronic service before challenging an e-summons's validity.

sections.title: Summons how served
sections.raw_text:
(1) Every summons shall be served by a police officer, or subject to such rules as the State Government may make in this behalf, by an officer of the Court issuing it or other public servant:
Provided that the police station or the registrar in the Court shall maintain a register to enter the address, email address, phone number and such other details as the State Government may, by rules, provide.
(2) The summons shall, if practicable, be served personally on the person summoned, by delivering or tendering to him one of the duplicates of the summons:
Provided that summons bearing the image of Court's seal may also be served by electronic communication in such form and in such manner, as the State Government may, by rules, provide.
(3) Every person on whom a summons is so served personally shall, if so required by the serving officer, sign a receipt therefor on the back of the other duplicate.

breakdown.plain_summary: Personal service is the default and preferred method — a duplicate handed or tendered directly to the summoned person, who may be asked to sign a receipt. Police officers, court officers, or other public servants may serve it. A new BNSS layer allows electronic service of a sealed summons per State Government rules, and mandates a register capturing address, email, and phone details to support that.
essential_elements: Personal service ('if practicable') is the primary mode — delivering/tendering a duplicate directly to the person.
Electronic service of a summons bearing the Court seal's image is now expressly permitted, per State Government rules.
A register of contact details (address, email, phone) must be maintained at the police station or Court registry.
The summoned person may be required to sign a receipt on the other duplicate.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Personal service is required only 'if practicable' — where impracticable, the later sections (65-71) provide alternative service modes.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the entry point for the whole service-of-summons cascade (Sections 64-71) — always check which specific mode was actually used and whether its preconditions (impracticability, due diligence, etc.) were genuinely satisfied before accepting service as valid.

sections.title: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies
sections.raw_text:
(1) Service of a summons on a company or corporation may be effected by serving it on the Director, Manager, Secretary or other officer of the company or corporation, or by letter sent by registered post addressed to the Director, Manager, Secretary or other officer of the company or corporation in India, in which case the service shall be deemed to have been effected when the letter would arrive in ordinary course of post.
Explanation.—In this section, "company" means a body corporate and "corporation" means an incorporated company or other body corporate registered under the Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013) or a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 (21 of 1860).
(2) Service of a summons on a firm or other association of individuals may be effected by serving it on any partner of such firm or association, or by letter sent by registered post addressed to such partner, in which case the service shall be deemed to have been effected when the letter would arrive in ordinary course of post.

breakdown.plain_summary: Sets out how to summon organisations rather than individuals: for companies/corporations, service on a Director/Manager/Secretary/other officer, or registered post to such a person, suffices — with a deeming rule that registered-post service is complete when the letter would ordinarily arrive, not when actually received. Firms/associations follow the same pattern via any partner.
essential_elements: Two alternative modes for companies/corporations: direct service on a named category of officer, or registered post addressed to such an officer.
'Company'/'corporation' expressly includes Companies Act, 2013 entities and Societies Registration Act, 1860 registered societies.
Registered-post service is deemed effected on ordinary-course arrival — an evidentiary presumption, not proof of actual receipt.
Firms/associations: service on any partner, personally or by registered post to that partner.
breakdown.how_to_read: The 'deemed service' rule on ordinary-course-of-post arrival is important — it shifts the burden onto the entity to show non-receipt was NOT due to ordinary postal course, rather than the prosecution having to prove actual receipt.

sections.title: Service when persons summoned cannot be found
sections.raw_text:
Where the person summoned cannot, by the exercise of due diligence, be found, the summons may be served by leaving one of the duplicates for him with some adult member of his family residing with him, and the person with whom the summons is so left shall, if so required by the serving officer, sign a receipt therefor on the back of the other duplicate.
Explanation.—A servant is not a member of the family within the meaning of this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: The first fallback when the person can't be personally found despite genuine effort: leave a duplicate with an adult family member residing with them. The Explanation deliberately excludes servants from counting as 'family' — service on domestic staff does not satisfy this provision.
essential_elements: Precondition: the person cannot be found despite 'due diligence' — a genuine, not token, search effort.
Service must be on an ADULT member of the family who resides WITH the summoned person.
A servant is expressly excluded from being treated as 'family' for this purpose.
breakdown.how_to_read: Challenges to substituted service under this section often turn on whether 'due diligence' was genuinely exercised before resorting to family-member service, and whether the recipient was truly an adult family member residing with the person (not a servant, neighbour, or non-resident relative).

sections.title: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided
sections.raw_text: If service cannot by the exercise of due diligence be effected as provided in section 64, section 65 or section 66, the serving officer shall affix one of the duplicates of the summons to some conspicuous part of the house or homestead in which the person summoned ordinarily resides; and thereupon the Court, after making such inquiries as it thinks fit, may either declare that the summons has been duly served or order fresh service in such manner as it considers proper.

breakdown.plain_summary: The second and final fallback — 'affixation' or 'pasting' service: if none of Sections 64-66 work, the officer pastes a duplicate on a visible part of the person's usual residence. This does not automatically count as valid service — the Court must independently inquire and either confirm it as duly served or order the process to be tried again differently.
essential_elements: Available only after due-diligence attempts under Sections 64, 65, and 66 have all failed.
Affixation must be to a conspicuous part of the house/homestead where the person ORDINARILY resides.
The Court retains an independent gatekeeping role — it must inquire and decide whether to declare service valid or order fresh service.
breakdown.how_to_read: Affixation ('paste') service is the most commonly challenged mode — always check whether the address was genuinely the person's ordinary residence and whether the Court actually conducted the required inquiry before declaring service valid, rather than mechanically accepting the officer's report.

sections.title: Service on Government servant
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where the person summoned is in the active service of the Government, the Court issuing the summons shall ordinarily send it in duplicate to the head of the office in which such person is employed; and such head shall thereupon cause the summons to be served in the manner provided by section 64, and shall return it to the Court under his signature with the endorsement required by that section.
(2) Such signature shall be evidence of due service.

breakdown.plain_summary: A special routing rule for government servants: rather than the usual direct service, the Court ordinarily channels the summons through the head of the employee's office, who serves it per Section 64 and returns it endorsed. The head's signature on that endorsement is itself treated as evidence that service was duly completed.
essential_elements: Applies where the summoned person is in active Government service.
Routing is via the head of the employing office, not direct service by the Court's own officer.
The head of office must serve per Section 64's method and return the summons endorsed and signed.
The head's signature is evidence of due service — a documentary shortcut for proving service.
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful where a government-servant accused disputes receipt of a summons — the office head's signed endorsement is strong, near-conclusive documentary proof of service under sub-section (2).

sections.title: Service of summons outside local limits
sections.raw_text: When a Court desires that a summons issued by it shall be served at any place outside its local jurisdiction, it shall ordinarily send such summons in duplicate to a Magistrate within whose local jurisdiction the person summoned resides, or is, to be there served.

breakdown.plain_summary: Cross-jurisdiction service: a Court cannot itself serve a summons outside its own territorial limits — it must route the duplicate summons to the Magistrate whose jurisdiction covers where the person resides or is, so that local Magistrate arranges service.
essential_elements: Applies whenever the place of intended service is outside the issuing Court's own local jurisdiction.
Routing is to the Magistrate with local jurisdiction over the person's residence or present location.
breakdown.how_to_read: Combine with Section 70 (proof of out-of-jurisdiction service) when tracking the paper trail for a summons served through another jurisdiction's Magistrate.

sections.title: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present
sections.raw_text:
(1) When a summons issued by a Court is served outside its local jurisdiction, and in any case where the officer who has served a summons is not present at the hearing of the case, an affidavit, purporting to be made before a Magistrate, that such summons has been served, and a duplicate of the summons purporting to be endorsed (in the manner provided by section 64 or section 66) by the person to whom it was delivered or tendered or with whom it was left, shall be admissible in evidence, and the statements made therein shall be deemed to be correct unless and until the contrary is proved.
(2) The affidavit mentioned in this section may be attached to the duplicate of the summons and returned to the Court.
(3) All summons served through electronic communication under sections 64 to 71 (both inclusive) shall be considered as duly served and a copy of such summons shall be attested and kept as a proof of service of summons.

breakdown.plain_summary: A practical evidence rule so cases aren't stalled waiting for the serving officer to personally testify every time: an affidavit before a Magistrate, plus an endorsed duplicate summons, is admissible proof of service, presumed correct unless disproved. Electronic-service summons under Sections 64-71 are treated as duly served once an attested copy is kept as proof.
essential_elements: Applies to out-of-jurisdiction service, or whenever the serving officer is unavailable at the hearing.
The affidavit + endorsed duplicate together are admissible evidence of service.
A rebuttable presumption of correctness attaches to the affidavit's statements ('unless and until the contrary is proved').
Electronically served summons are deemed duly served upon attestation and retention of a copy as proof.
breakdown.how_to_read: The presumption of correctness is rebuttable, not conclusive — a person genuinely disputing service can still lead evidence to displace the affidavit's presumption; this section eases the prosecution's evidentiary burden but does not foreclose challenge.

sections.title: Service of summons on witness
sections.raw_text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the preceding sections of this Chapter, a Court issuing a summons to a witness may, in addition to and simultaneously with the issue of such summons, direct a copy of the summons to be served by electronic communication or by registered post addressed to the witness at the place where he ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain.
(2) When an acknowledgement purporting to be signed by the witness or an endorsement purporting to be made by a postal employee that the witness refused to take delivery of the summons has been received or on the proof of delivery of summons under sub-section (3) of section 70 by electronic communication to the satisfaction of the Court, the Court issuing summons may deem that the summons has been duly served.

breakdown.plain_summary: A witness-specific fast track: the Court can send a parallel copy of the witness summons by electronic communication or registered post, on top of the usual modes. If a signed acknowledgement comes back, or the postal employee notes a refusal to accept delivery, or electronic delivery is proved under Section 70(3), the Court may treat the summons as duly served — a practical mechanism to speed up witness attendance without waiting for personal service to succeed or fail.
essential_elements: Available specifically for witness summonses (not accused-person summonses generally).
Operates 'in addition to and simultaneously with' the ordinary summons — a parallel, not exclusive, channel.
Deemed service arises from: a signed acknowledgement, a postal refusal endorsement, or proved electronic delivery under Section 70(3).
Closes Part A of Chapter VI (Summons); Part B (Warrant of Arrest) follows from Section 72.
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful where a witness is evading personal service — the parallel electronic/registered-post channel under this section, once acknowledgement or proved delivery is shown, lets the Court proceed without waiting indefinitely for personal service.

sections.title: Form of warrant of arrest and duration
sections.raw_text:
(1) Every warrant of arrest issued by a Court under this Sanhita shall be in writing, signed by the presiding officer of such Court and shall bear the seal of the Court.
(2) Every such warrant shall remain in force until it is cancelled by the Court which issued it, or until it is executed.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Part B (Warrant of Arrest). A warrant must be written, signed by the presiding officer, and sealed. Unlike a summons that may lapse, a warrant is open-ended in duration — it stays valid indefinitely until the issuing Court cancels it or it is actually executed, whichever comes first.
essential_elements: Formal requirements: writing, signature of the presiding officer, Court seal.
Duration: continuously in force, with no expiry date, until cancellation by the issuing Court or execution.
breakdown.how_to_read: Because a warrant doesn't expire on its own, an old, unexecuted warrant can resurface years later — always check the case record for whether it was ever formally cancelled before assuming it has lapsed.

sections.title: Power to direct security to be taken

breakdown.plain_summary: Lets a Court build a release-on-bail mechanism directly into the warrant itself: an endorsement on the warrant can direct the executing officer to release the arrested person immediately upon their furnishing a bail bond with sufficient sureties, without needing to wait for a separate Court appearance. The endorsement must specify the number of sureties, the bound amount, and the attendance time.
essential_elements: This is discretionary ('may'), not mandatory, on the issuing Court.
The endorsement must specify: number of sureties, the amount each (and the arrested person) is bound in, and the attendance time.
The executing officer, upon receiving the bond, must forward it to the Court.
breakdown.how_to_read: A 'bailable warrant' endorsement under this section is a practical tool to avoid unnecessary custody for persons the Court is willing to release on conditions — check any arrest warrant for such an endorsement before assuming custody is mandatory pending Court appearance.

sections.title: Warrants to whom directed
sections.raw_text:
(1) A warrant of arrest shall ordinarily be directed to one or more police officers; but the Court issuing such a warrant may, if its immediate execution is necessary and no police officer is immediately available, direct it to any other person or persons, and such person or persons shall execute the same.
(2) When a warrant is directed to more officers or persons than one, it may be executed by all, or by any one or more of them.

breakdown.plain_summary: The default executor of a warrant is a police officer, but the Court has a fallback power to direct it to any other person if urgent execution is needed and no police officer is immediately available. Where multiple officers/persons are named, any one or more of them (not necessarily all) can carry out the execution.
essential_elements: Default: directed to one or more police officers.
Fallback to non-police persons requires both urgency (immediate execution necessary) and unavailability of a police officer.
Multiple addressees may execute jointly or individually — execution by any one or more suffices.
breakdown.how_to_read: The non-police fallback is genuinely exceptional — challenge any warrant executed by a private person where the urgency/unavailability preconditions are not documented.

sections.title: Warrant may be directed to any person
sections.raw_text:
(1) The Chief Judicial Magistrate or a Magistrate of the first class may direct a warrant to any person within his local jurisdiction for the arrest of any escaped convict, proclaimed offender or of any person who is accused of a non-bailable offence and is evading arrest.
(2) Such person shall acknowledge in writing the receipt of the warrant, and shall execute it if the person for whose arrest it was issued, is in, or enters on, any land or other property under his charge.
(3) When the person against whom such warrant is issued is arrested, he shall be made over with the warrant to the nearest police officer, who shall cause him to be taken before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, unless security is taken under section 73.

breakdown.plain_summary: A narrower, higher-threshold version of the private-person warrant power: only a Chief Judicial Magistrate or first-class Magistrate can invoke it, and only for specific hard categories of person — escaped convicts, proclaimed offenders, or non-bailable-offence accused persons who are evading arrest. The directed person must acknowledge the warrant in writing and executes it only if the target is on land/property under their charge, then hands the arrested person over with the warrant to the nearest police officer.
essential_elements: Issuing authority limited to CJM or first-class Magistrate, acting within their local jurisdiction.
Target categories are specific: escaped convicts, proclaimed offenders, or evading non-bailable-offence accused.
The directed person must acknowledge receipt of the warrant in writing.
Execution power is triggered only when the target is on, or enters, land/property under the directed person's charge.
After arrest, the person must be made over with the warrant to the nearest police officer for production before a jurisdictional Magistrate (unless Section 73 security is taken).
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a targeted tool for landholders/persons-in-charge of property against whom an escapee or proclaimed offender may take refuge — distinct from the general Section 74 fallback, and correspondingly narrower in scope.

sections.title: Warrant directed to police officer
sections.raw_text: A warrant directed to any police officer may also be executed by any other police officer whose name is endorsed upon the warrant by the officer to whom it is directed or endorsed.

breakdown.plain_summary: Allows onward delegation within the police: an officer who receives a warrant can pass execution authority to another named officer simply by endorsing that officer's name onto the warrant — no fresh Court order is needed for this internal transfer.
essential_elements: Delegation chain: original addressee officer endorses another officer's name; that new officer may then execute.
The endorsement chain can continue — 'the officer to whom it is directed or endorsed' can itself further endorse.
breakdown.how_to_read: Check the endorsement chain on the physical/digital warrant when an arrest is executed by an officer other than the one originally named — a missing or improper endorsement is a technical defect worth raising.

sections.title: Notification of substance of warrant
sections.raw_text: The police officer or other person executing a warrant of arrest shall notify the substance thereof to the person to be arrested, and, if so required, shall show him the warrant.

breakdown.plain_summary: Mirrors the disclosure duty for summons-delegation (Section 55) but for warrants generally: the executing officer must tell the person the substance of the warrant, and show the actual warrant document if the person asks.
essential_elements: Disclosure of the substance of the warrant is mandatory in every execution.
Showing the physical/digital warrant itself is required only if the arrested person asks for it.
breakdown.how_to_read: A failure to notify the substance of the warrant, especially where the person specifically demanded to see it and was refused, is a clean procedural irregularity to raise on the legality of the arrest.

sections.title: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay
sections.raw_text:
The police officer or other person executing a warrant of arrest shall (subject to the provisions of section 73 as to security) without unnecessary delay bring the person arrested before the Court before which he is required by law to produce such person:
Provided that such delay shall not, in any case, exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: The warrant-arrest counterpart to Sections 57-58's production and 24-hour rules for warrantless arrests: production before the Court must happen without unnecessary delay, and in any event within 24 hours (excluding travel time) — unless the person was released on Section 73 security instead.
essential_elements: Applies to arrests made under a warrant.
Subject to Section 73 — if security/bail bond was taken and the person released, this production duty doesn't require custodial production.
Outer limit: 24 hours, exclusive of journey time, mirroring Section 58's warrantless-arrest rule.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 24-hour clock is displaced entirely where Section 73 security has already resulted in release.
breakdown.how_to_read: This confirms the 24-hour production discipline applies uniformly whether the arrest is with or without a warrant (Sections 58 and 78 read together) — a useful symmetry to cite when challenging any prolonged pre-production custody regardless of arrest type.

sections.title: Where warrant may be executed
sections.raw_text: A warrant of arrest may be executed at any place in India.

breakdown.plain_summary: A short but important jurisdictional rule: a warrant is not confined to the issuing Court's own territory — it can be executed anywhere in India, subject to the endorsement/forwarding mechanics of Sections 80-81 for out-of-jurisdiction execution.
essential_elements: No territorial limit on where a warrant may be executed within India.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair with Sections 80 and 81, which set out the specific mechanics (forwarding, endorsement) for actually executing a warrant outside the issuing Court's jurisdiction.

sections.title: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction
sections.raw_text:
(1) When a warrant is to be executed outside the local jurisdiction of the Court issuing it, such Court may, instead of directing the warrant to a police officer within its jurisdiction, forward it by post or otherwise to any Executive Magistrate or District Superintendent of Police or Commissioner of Police within the local limits of whose jurisdiction it is to be executed; and the Executive Magistrate or District Superintendent or Commissioner shall endorse his name thereon, and if practicable, cause it to be executed in the manner hereinbefore provided.
(2) The Court issuing a warrant under sub-section (1) shall forward, along with the warrant, the substance of the information against the person to be arrested together with such documents, if any, as may be sufficient to enable the Court acting under section 83 to decide whether bail should or should not be granted to the person.

breakdown.plain_summary: One method of cross-jurisdiction execution: the issuing Court forwards the warrant to an Executive Magistrate, District Superintendent of Police, or Commissioner of Police in the execution district, who endorses it and arranges execution. Crucially, the issuing Court must also forward the case information and supporting documents so that the Section 83 Magistrate at the other end can make an informed bail decision.
essential_elements: Applies when execution must happen outside the issuing Court's local jurisdiction.
Forwarding target: Executive Magistrate, District Superintendent of Police, or Commissioner of Police of the execution district.
The receiving officer endorses the warrant and, if practicable, arranges execution.
The issuing Court MUST forward case information/documents sufficient for a bail decision under Section 83 — a mandatory information-sharing duty.
breakdown.how_to_read: If bail is refused or delayed at the Section 83 stage because the receiving officer lacked adequate information, check whether the issuing Court actually complied with its sub-section (2) documentation duty — a lapse here can be a basis to expedite or reconsider bail.

sections.title: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction
sections.raw_text:
(1) When a warrant directed to a police officer is to be executed beyond the local jurisdiction of the Court issuing the same, he shall ordinarily take it for endorsement either to an Executive Magistrate or to a police officer not below the rank of an officer in charge of a police station, within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the warrant is to be executed.
(2) Such Magistrate or police officer shall endorse his name thereon and such endorsement shall be sufficient authority to the police officer to whom the warrant is directed to execute the same, and the local police shall, if so required, assist such officer in executing such warrant.
(3) Whenever there is reason to believe that the delay occasioned by obtaining the endorsement of the Magistrate or police officer within whose local jurisdiction the warrant is to be executed will prevent such execution, the police officer to whom it is directed may execute the same without such endorsement in any place beyond the local jurisdiction of the Court which issued it.

breakdown.plain_summary: A second, officer-carried method of cross-jurisdiction execution (as opposed to Section 80's Court-forwarded method): the police officer holding the warrant personally takes it to the local Executive Magistrate or a station-house-officer-or-above ranked police officer for endorsement, which then authorises execution with local police assistance. An urgency exception lets the officer skip the endorsement entirely if waiting for it would defeat execution.
essential_elements: Applies specifically where the warrant is directed to a police officer who must execute it outside the issuing Court's jurisdiction.
Endorsement is sought from either an Executive Magistrate or a police officer of officer-in-charge rank or above, local to the execution area.
The endorsement authorises execution and entitles the officer to local police assistance if needed.
Urgency exception: if the endorsement delay would defeat execution, the officer may execute without it anywhere beyond the issuing Court's jurisdiction.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The urgency exception in sub-section (3) is a genuine departure from the normal endorsement requirement, not merely a convenience option.
breakdown.how_to_read: Where a warrant is executed without endorsement under the urgency exception, the 'reason to believe' delay-would-defeat-execution standard should be scrutinised — it is the sole legal basis for bypassing the ordinarily mandatory endorsement step.

sections.title: Procedure on arrest of person against whom warrant issued
sections.raw_text:
(1) When a warrant of arrest is executed outside the district in which it was issued, the person arrested shall, unless the Court which issued the warrant is within thirty kilometres of the place of arrest or is nearer than the Executive Magistrate or District Superintendent of Police or Commissioner of Police within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the arrest was made, or unless security is taken under section 73, be taken before such Magistrate or District Superintendent or Commissioner.
(2) On the arrest of any person referred to in sub-section (1), the police officer shall forthwith give the information regarding such arrest and the place where the arrested person is being held to the designated police officer in the district and to such officer of another district where the arrested person normally resides.

breakdown.plain_summary: Governs what happens right after an out-of-district warrant arrest: ordinarily the person is taken before the local Executive Magistrate/DSP/Commissioner rather than all the way back to the issuing Court — unless the issuing Court is actually closer (within 30 km or nearer than the local officer), or Section 73 security has already been taken. The arrest must also be immediately reported to the designated police officer both in the arrest district and in the person's home district.
essential_elements: Default: production before the local Executive Magistrate/DSP/Commissioner of the arrest district.
Exception 1: issuing Court is within 30 km of the arrest place, or nearer than the local officer — then production may go directly to the issuing Court instead.
Exception 2: Section 73 security already taken — no custodial production required.
Mandatory dual notification: designated police officer of the arrest district AND of the arrested person's normal-residence district.
breakdown.how_to_read: The dual-district notification duty under sub-section (2) is a genuinely new BNSS safeguard (linked to Section 37's designated-officer/control-room scheme) aimed at making arrest information traceable to family/counsel even when the arrest happens far from home — check both notifications were made where custody location is disputed.

sections.title: Procedure by Magistrate before whom such person arrested is brought
sections.raw_text:
(1) The Executive Magistrate or District Superintendent of Police or Commissioner of Police shall, if the person arrested appears to be the person intended by the Court which issued the warrant, direct his removal in custody to such Court:
Provided that, if the offence is bailable, and such person is ready and willing to give bail bond to the satisfaction of such Magistrate, District Superintendent or Commissioner, or a direction has been endorsed under section 73 on the warrant and such person is ready and willing to give the security required by such direction, the Magistrate, District Superintendent or Commissioner shall take such bail bond or security, as the case may be, and forward the bond, to the Court which issued the warrant:
Provided further that if the offence is a non-bailable one, it shall be lawful for the Chief Judicial Magistrate (subject to the provisions of section 480), or the Sessions Judge, of the district in which the arrest is made on consideration of the information and the documents referred to in sub-section (2) of section 80, to release such person on bail.
(2) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to prevent a police officer from taking security under section 73.

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes Part B (Warrant of Arrest). The receiving Magistrate/DSP/Commissioner must first confirm identity, then ordinarily order custodial removal to the issuing Court — but two provisos create local bail routes instead: if the offence is bailable and the person is willing to furnish bail (or a Section 73 endorsement already covers it), bail is taken locally and the bond forwarded to the issuing Court; and even for a non-bailable offence, the local Chief Judicial Magistrate or Sessions Judge may grant bail based on the information/documents the issuing Court forwarded under Section 80(2).
essential_elements: Identity confirmation ('appears to be the person intended by the Court') is the threshold step.
Default outcome: custodial removal to the issuing Court.
First proviso: bailable offence + willingness to furnish bail (or existing Section 73 direction) → local bail bond taken and forwarded, no custodial removal needed.
Second proviso: even non-bailable offences allow local bail by the CJM (subject to Section 480) or Sessions Judge, based on the Section 80(2) forwarded documents.
Sub-section (2) preserves the independent Section 73 security-taking power for police officers.
breakdown.how_to_read: The second proviso's local-bail-even-for-non-bailable-offences route is a significant practical relief mechanism for persons arrested far from the issuing Court — always check whether the issuing Court actually forwarded adequate Section 80(2) documentation, since the local Magistrate's bail decision depends entirely on that information reaching them.

sections.title: Proclamation for person absconding

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Part C (Proclamation and Attachment). Where a warrant can't be executed because the accused has absconded or is hiding, the Court can publicly proclaim, giving at least 30 days' notice to appear, published via public reading, affixation at the person's residence and the courthouse, and optionally a newspaper notice. A Court's own written statement that publication happened is conclusive proof of compliance. For serious offences (10+ years, life, or death-punishable), continued non-appearance lets the Court formally declare the person a 'proclaimed offender' — a status with independent legal consequences elsewhere in the Sanhita and beyond.
essential_elements: Trigger: Court's reason to believe the warrant cannot be executed due to absconding/concealment.
Minimum notice period: not less than 30 days from the date of publication.
Mandatory publication modes: public reading in the town/village, affixation at the residence, and affixation at the courthouse; newspaper publication is discretionary, not mandatory.
A Court's written statement of due publication is CONCLUSIVE evidence of compliance — not merely rebuttable.

Proclaimed-offender declaration is available only for offences carrying 10+ years, life imprisonment, or death, and only after the person fails to appear as required and after such inquiry as the Court thinks fit.
breakdown.how_to_read: The 'conclusive evidence' status of the Court's publication statement under sub-section (3) is a high evidentiary bar — it forecloses ordinary challenge to whether publication actually occurred, so any challenge to a proclaimed-offender declaration should instead target the underlying preconditions (offence severity threshold, adequacy of the inquiry under sub-section (4)) rather than publication itself.

sections.title: Attachment of property of person absconding
sections.raw_text:
(1) The Court issuing a proclamation under section 84 may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, at any time after the issue of the proclamation, order the attachment of any property, movable or immovable, or both, belonging to the proclaimed person:
Provided that where at the time of the issue of the proclamation the Court is satisfied, by affidavit or otherwise, that the person in relation to whom the proclamation is to be issued—
(a) is about to dispose of the whole or any part of his property; or
(b) is about to remove the whole or any part of his property from the local jurisdiction of the Court, it may order the attachment of property simultaneously with the issue of the proclamation.
(2) Such order shall authorise the attachment of any property belonging to such person within the district in which it is made; and it shall authorise the attachment of any property belonging to such person without such district when endorsed by the District Magistrate within whose district such property is situate.
(3) If the property ordered to be attached is a debt or other movable property, the attachment under this section shall be made—
(a) by seizure; or
(b) by the appointment of a receiver; or
(c) by an order in writing prohibiting the delivery of such property to the proclaimed person or to any one on his behalf; or
(d) by all or any two of such methods, as the Court thinks fit.
(4) If the property ordered to be attached is immovable, the attachment under this section shall, in the case of land paying revenue to the State Government, be made through the Collector of the district in which the land is situate, and in all other cases—
(a) by taking possession; or
(b) by the appointment of a receiver; or
(c) by an order in writing prohibiting the payment of rent on delivery of property to the proclaimed person or to any one on his behalf; or
(d) by all or any two of such methods, as the Court thinks fit.
(5) If the property ordered to be attached consists of live-stock or is of a perishable nature, the Court may, if it thinks it expedient, order immediate sale thereof, and in such case the proceeds of the sale shall abide the order of the Court.
(6) The powers, duties and liabilities of a receiver appointed under this section shall be the same as those of a receiver appointed under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908).

breakdown.plain_summary: Gives the Court teeth to pressure a proclaimed absconder back to Court by attaching their property. Ordinarily attachment follows the proclamation (with reasons recorded in writing), but if the Court is satisfied the person is about to dump or move their assets out of jurisdiction, attachment can happen simultaneously with the proclamation itself. The mechanics differ for movable property (seizure, receiver, or a delivery-prohibition order) versus immovable property (possession, receiver, or rent-prohibition order, with the Collector's involvement for revenue-paying land). Perishables/livestock may be sold immediately, proceeds held pending the Court's order.
essential_elements: Attachment requires reasons recorded in writing by the issuing Court.
Normally attachment follows the proclamation; the proviso allows simultaneous attachment only on satisfaction (by affidavit or otherwise) that the person is about to dispose of or remove property.
Territorial scope: automatic within the issuing district; outside the district only with the local District Magistrate's endorsement.
Movable property: seizure, receiver appointment, or delivery-prohibition order (or a combination).
Immovable property: Collector-routed for revenue land; otherwise possession, receiver, or rent-prohibition order (or a combination).
Perishables/livestock may be sold immediately, with proceeds held subject to the Court's order.
A receiver appointed here has the same powers, duties and liabilities as a CPC, 1908 receiver.
breakdown.how_to_read: The CPC cross-reference in sub-section (6) means the entire body of civil-procedure receiver jurisprudence (accounting duties, security, removal for misconduct) applies to a criminal-proceeding attachment receiver — a useful body of law to invoke in property-attachment disputes.

sections.title: Identification and attachment of property of proclaimed person
sections.raw_text: The Court may, on the written request from a police officer not below the rank of the Superintendent of Police or Commissioner of Police, initiate the process of requesting assistance from a Court or an authority in the contracting State for identification, attachment and forfeiture of property belonging to a proclaimed person in accordance with the procedure provided in Chapter VIII.

breakdown.plain_summary: A cross-border extension unique to the BNSS's international-cooperation architecture: where a proclaimed offender's property is abroad, a senior police officer (SP/Commissioner rank or above) can trigger a formal request, via the Court, to a foreign 'contracting State' for help identifying, attaching, and forfeiting that property — using the reciprocal-arrangement machinery set out fully in Chapter VIII.
essential_elements: Trigger: written request from a police officer of SP or Commissioner of Police rank or above.
Subject matter: identification, attachment, and forfeiture of a proclaimed person's property located in a contracting State.
Procedural mechanism: governed by, and must follow, the Chapter VIII reciprocal-arrangements procedure.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is a gateway provision, not a self-contained procedure — always read it together with Chapter VIII for the actual mechanics of the request and the definition of 'contracting State.'

sections.title: Claims and objections to attachment
sections.raw_text:
(1) If any claim is preferred to, or objection made to the attachment of, any property attached under section 85, within six months from the date of such attachment, by any person other than the proclaimed person, on the ground that the claimant or objector has an interest in such property, and that such interest is not liable to attachment under section 85, the claim or objection shall be inquired into, and may be allowed or disallowed in whole or in part:
Provided that any claim preferred or objection made within the period allowed by this sub-section may, in the event of the death of the claimant or objector, be continued by his legal representative.
(2) Claims or objections under sub-section (1) may be preferred or made in the Court by which the order of attachment is issued, or, if the claim or objection is in respect of property attached under an order endorsed under sub-section (2) of section 85, in the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate of the district in which the attachment is made.
(3) Every such claim or objection shall be inquired into by the Court in which it is preferred or made:
Provided that, if it is preferred or made in the Court of a Chief Judicial Magistrate, he may make it over for disposal to any Magistrate subordinate to him.
(4) Any person whose claim or objection has been disallowed in whole or in part by an order under sub-section (1) may, within a period of one year from the date of such order, institute a suit to establish the right which he claims in respect of the property in dispute; but subject to the result of such suit, if any, the order shall be conclusive.

breakdown.plain_summary: Protects third parties (not the absconder) who genuinely have an interest in attached property: they have a 6-month window from attachment to raise a claim or objection, which the Court must inquire into. If disallowed, the claimant isn't shut out entirely — they get a further one-year window to file a civil suit to establish their right; until then, the attachment order stands as conclusive.
essential_elements: Time limit for the claim/objection itself: 6 months from the date of attachment.
Only persons OTHER THAN the proclaimed person may claim/object, on the ground of their own interest not liable to attachment.
A claimant/objector who dies during the permitted period may be substituted by their legal representative.
Forum: the attaching Court, or (for cross-district endorsed attachments) the CJM of the attachment district, who may delegate disposal to a subordinate Magistrate.
If disallowed, a further civil suit may be filed within one year of the disallowance order to establish the right.
The disallowance order is conclusive unless and until displaced by the outcome of that civil suit.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is essentially a summary claims-adjudication mechanism with a civil-suit safety valve — third parties should not assume the 6-month claim process is their only recourse; a disallowed claim survives as a civil cause of action for a further year.

sections.title: Release, sale and restoration of attached property
sections.raw_text:
(1) If the proclaimed person appears within the time specified in the proclamation, the Court shall make an order releasing the property from the attachment.
(2) If the proclaimed person does not appear within the time specified in the proclamation, the property under the attachment shall be at the disposal of the State Government; but it shall not be sold until the expiration of six months from the date of the attachment and until any claim preferred or objection made under section 87 has been disposed of under that section, unless it is subject to speedy and natural decay, or the Court considers that the sale would be for the benefit of the owner; in either of which cases the Court may cause it to be sold whenever it thinks fit.
(3) If, within two years from the date of the attachment, any person whose property is or has been at the disposal of the State Government under sub-section (2), appears voluntarily or is apprehended and brought before the Court by whose order the property was attached, or the Court to which such Court is subordinate, and proves to the satisfaction of such Court that he did not abscond or conceal himself for the purpose of avoiding execution of the warrant, and that he had not such notice of the proclamation as to enable him to attend within the time specified therein, such property, or, if the same has been sold, the net proceeds of the sale, or, if part only thereof has been sold, the net proceeds of the sale and the residue of the property, shall, after satisfying therefrom all costs incurred in consequence of the attachment, be delivered to him.

breakdown.plain_summary: The end-of-life scheme for attached property: if the absconder shows up on time, the attachment is released outright. If not, the property passes to State Government disposal, but a 6-month sale moratorium applies (pending claims disposal under Section 87), except for perishables or where sale would clearly benefit the owner. Crucially, even after State disposal, a genuine absconder who returns within 2 years and proves they weren't deliberately evading and genuinely lacked adequate notice can recover the property (or its sale proceeds, minus attachment costs) — the scheme isn't a permanent forfeiture by default.
essential_elements: Timely appearance within the proclamation period → automatic release of attachment.
Non-appearance → property goes to State Government disposal, but sale is deferred at least 6 months and pending Section 87 claims disposal, unless the perishable/owner-benefit exceptions apply.
2-year restoration window: the person must prove BOTH that they did not abscond/conceal to avoid the warrant AND that they lacked adequate notice of the proclamation to appear in time.
Restoration is of the property itself, or net sale proceeds (plus any unsold residue), after deducting attachment costs.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Perishable/livestock property, or property whose immediate sale the Court considers beneficial to the owner, can be sold immediately notwithstanding the 6-month moratorium.
breakdown.how_to_read: The 2-year restoration route under sub-section (3) is a critical safety net often overlooked — someone who was genuinely unaware of proceedings (e.g., no valid notice reached them) is not automatically stripped of their property forever merely because they didn't appear in time.

sections.title: Appeal from order rejecting application for restoration of attached property
sections.raw_text: Any person referred to in sub-section (3) of section 88, who is aggrieved by any refusal to deliver property or the proceeds of the sale thereof may appeal to the Court to which appeals ordinarily lie from the sentences of the first-mentioned Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes Part C. If a Section 88(3) restoration application is refused, the aggrieved person isn't left without recourse — they can appeal to whichever Court normally hears appeals from sentences of the Court that refused restoration.
essential_elements: Available only to a person covered by Section 88(3) (i.e., someone who applied for restoration and was refused).
The appellate forum is determined by reference to the ordinary sentence-appeal hierarchy from the refusing Court — no separate special forum is created.
breakdown.how_to_read: A straightforward but easily missed remedy — always check whether a restoration refusal under Section 88(3) has been properly appealed under this section before treating it as final.

sections.title: Issue of warrant in lieu of, or in addition to, summons
sections.raw_text:
A Court may, in any case in which it is empowered by this Sanhita to issue a summons for the appearance of any person, issue, after recording its reasons in writing, a warrant for his arrest—
(a) if, either before the issue of such summons, or after the issue of the same but before the time fixed for his appearance, the Court sees reason to believe that he has absconded or will not obey the summons; or
(b) if at such time he fails to appear and the summons is proved to have been duly served in time to admit of his appearing in accordance therewith and no reasonable excuse is offered for such failure.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Part D. A Court that could ordinarily use a summons may instead (or additionally) escalate to a warrant — but only with reasons recorded in writing, and only in two specific situations: reasonable belief the person will abscond or defy the summons (before or after issuing it), or actual non-appearance despite proven timely service and no reasonable excuse.
essential_elements: Escalation from summons to warrant requires reasons recorded in writing — a mandatory documentation safeguard against arbitrary escalation.
Ground (a): reasonable belief of absconding or non-compliance, assessable either before or after the summons is issued.
Ground (b): actual failure to appear, PROVEN due service in time, and absence of a reasonable excuse — all three must be satisfied together.
breakdown.how_to_read: The 'reasons recorded in writing' requirement is the key check on this power — where a warrant issues under ground (b) without proof of due, timely service, or where a reasonable excuse was offered but ignored, that escalation is vulnerable to challenge.

sections.title: Power to take bond or bail bond for appearance
sections.raw_text: When any person for whose appearance or arrest the officer presiding in any Court is empowered to issue a summons or warrant, is present in such Court, such officer may require such person to execute a bond or bail bond for his appearance in such Court, or any other Court to which the case may be transferred for trial.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where the person is already physically present in Court (whether they came voluntarily or were produced), the Court can simply require a bond or bail bond for future appearance — covering both the current Court and any Court the case might later be transferred to — without needing to formally go through the summons/warrant process at all.
essential_elements: Applies only where the person is already present before the Court empowered to issue a summons/warrant for them.
The bond/bail bond secures appearance not just in the present Court but also in any transferee Court for trial.
breakdown.how_to_read: A practical, low-friction tool — often used when an accused voluntarily appears, avoiding the need for a fresh summons/warrant cycle to secure their future attendance.

sections.title: Arrest on breach of bond or bail bond for appearance
sections.raw_text: When any person who is bound by any bond or bail bond taken under this Sanhita to appear before a Court, does not appear, the officer presiding in such Court may issue a warrant directing that such person be arrested and produced before him.

breakdown.plain_summary: The enforcement backstop for Sections 91 and every other bond/bail-bond-for-appearance provision in the Sanhita: if the bound person simply doesn't show up, the presiding officer can issue a warrant to have them arrested and brought before the Court. Closes Chapter VI (Processes to Compel Appearance).
essential_elements: Applies to any bond or bail bond taken 'under this Sanhita' for appearance — not limited to Section 91 bonds specifically.
Trigger is simple non-appearance; no separate finding of wilful default is textually required before the warrant may issue.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the general breach-of-appearance-bond remedy that operates across the whole Sanhita — cite it whenever any appearance bond (not just Section 91's) is broken, since it isn't confined to a single specific bond-creating provision.

sections.title: Provisions of this Chapter generally applicable to summons and warrants of arrest
sections.raw_text: The provisions contained in this Chapter relating to summons and warrant, and their issue, service and execution, shall, so far as may be, apply to every summons and every warrant of arrest issued under this Sanhita.

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes Chapter VI with a generalisation clause: everything Chapter VI says about how summonses and warrants are issued, served, and executed isn't limited to the specific proceedings described there — it applies, with necessary adaptation ('so far as may be'), to every summons and arrest warrant issued anywhere else in the Sanhita.
essential_elements: Extends Chapter VI's issue/service/execution machinery to ALL summonses and arrest warrants under the Sanhita, not just those arising directly under this Chapter.
The qualifier 'so far as may be' allows adaptation where a provision doesn't neatly fit a different context, rather than rigid literal application.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the statutory hook that lets practitioners invoke Chapter VI's detailed service/execution safeguards (e.g., the 24-hour rule, endorsement requirements) whenever a summons or warrant appears anywhere else in the Sanhita, even where that other provision doesn't spell out its own procedure.

sections.title: Summons to produce document or other thing
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whenever any Court or any officer in charge of a police station considers that the production of any document, electronic communication, including communication devices, which is likely to contain digital evidence or other thing is necessary or desirable for the purposes of any investigation, inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Sanhita by or before such Court or officer, such Court may issue a summons or such officer may, by a written order, either in physical form or in electronic form, require the person in whose possession or power such document or thing is believed to be, to attend and produce it, or to produce it, at the time and place stated in the summons or order.
(2) Any person required under this section merely to produce a document, or other thing shall be deemed to have complied with the requisition if he causes such document or thing to be produced instead of attending personally to produce the same.
(3) Nothing in this section shall be deemed—
(a) to affect sections 129 and 130 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 or the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 (13 of 1891); or
(b) to apply to a letter, postcard, or other document or any parcel or thing in the custody of the postal authority.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Chapter VII (Processes to Compel Production of Things), Part A. Either a Court or a station house officer can compel production of a document, thing, or — a notable BNSS addition — electronic communication/communication devices likely to contain digital evidence, by summons (Court) or written order (police officer), in physical or electronic form. Merely causing the item to be produced satisfies the requirement — personal attendance isn't required if production alone is achieved. Bankers' Books Evidence Act procedures and postal-custody items are expressly carved out (the latter handled instead by Section 95).
essential_elements: Issuing authority: any Court, or any officer in charge of a police station.
Subject matter expressly includes electronic communication and communication devices likely to contain digital evidence — a BNSS-specific modernisation.
The summons/order may itself be issued in physical or electronic form.
Compliance is satisfied by causing production, without personal attendance, for mere-production requisitions.
Express carve-outs: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam ss.129-130 and Bankers' Books Evidence Act procedures remain unaffected; postal-custody items are excluded (see Section 95 instead).
breakdown.how_to_read: The explicit inclusion of 'communication devices... likely to contain digital evidence' is a significant modernisation over the old CrPC's Section 91 — expect this to be the primary statutory basis for phone/laptop production orders in criminal investigations going forward.

sections.title: Procedure as to letters
sections.raw_text:
(1) If any document, parcel or thing in the custody of a postal authority is, in the opinion of the District Magistrate, Chief Judicial Magistrate, Court of Session or High Court wanted for the purpose of any investigation, inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Sanhita, such Magistrate or Court may require the postal authority to deliver the document, parcel or thing to such person as the Magistrate or Court directs.
(2) If any such document, parcel or thing is, in the opinion of any other Magistrate, whether Executive or Judicial, or of any Commissioner of Police or District Superintendent of Police, wanted for any such purpose, he may require the postal authority to cause search to be made for and to detain such document, parcel or thing pending the order of a District Magistrate, Chief Judicial Magistrate or Court under sub-section (1).

breakdown.plain_summary: The dedicated mechanism (excluded from Section 94) for items in postal custody: only the more senior authorities — DM, CJM, Sessions Court, or High Court — can directly order delivery of a postal item. Other Magistrates or senior police officers (Commissioner/DSP) have a lesser power: they can only require the postal authority to search for and hold the item pending a proper delivery order from one of the senior authorities.
essential_elements: Full delivery-direction power is reserved to DM, CJM, Sessions Court, or High Court.

Lesser 'search and detain' power is available to any other Magistrate (Executive or Judicial) or to a Commissioner of Police/District Superintendent of Police — but only pending an order from the senior authority.
breakdown.how_to_read: A two-tier structure deliberately restricts final control over postal items to senior judicial/executive authorities — a request routed only through a junior Magistrate or police officer cannot itself result in delivery, only detention pending a proper order.

sections.title: When search-warrant may be issued
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where—
(a) any Court has reason to believe that a person to whom a summons order under section 94 or a requisition under sub-section (1) of section 95 has been, or might be, addressed, will not or would not produce the document or thing as required by such summons or requisition; or
(b) such document or thing is not known to the Court to be in the possession of any person; or
(c) the Court considers that the purposes of any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Sanhita will be served by a general search or inspection,
it may issue a search-warrant; and the person to whom such warrant is directed, may search or inspect in accordance therewith and the provisions hereinafter contained.
(2) The Court may, if it thinks fit, specify in the warrant the particular place or part thereof to which only the search or inspection shall extend; and the person charged with the execution of such warrant shall then search or inspect only the place or part so specified.
(3) Nothing contained in this section shall authorise any Magistrate other than a District Magistrate or Chief Judicial Magistrate to grant a warrant to search for a document, parcel or other thing in the custody of the postal authority.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Part B (Search-warrants). A Court may escalate straight to a search-warrant in three situations: expected non-compliance with a Section 94/95 summons, the item's possessor being unknown, or the Court concluding a general search/inspection would serve the proceeding's purposes. The warrant can be scoped to a specific place/part of a place. Postal-custody searches remain specially restricted — only a DM or CJM can authorise those, consistent with Section 95's senior-authority-only scheme.
essential_elements: Three independent grounds for issuing a search-warrant: (a) anticipated non-production, (b) unknown possessor, or (c) general-search purpose.
The Court may limit the warrant's scope to a specified place or part of a place.
Postal-item searches remain restricted to DM/CJM level authorisation, mirroring Section 95's structure.
breakdown.how_to_read: Ground (c) — 'general search or inspection' — is the broadest of the three and the one most likely to be challenged as overbroad; always check whether the warrant is scoped under sub-section (2) or left dangerously open-ended.

sections.title: Search of place suspected to contain stolen property, forged documents, etc.

breakdown.plain_summary: A specialised, broader-than-usual search-warrant power for places suspected of harbouring stolen property or a defined list of 'objectionable articles' (counterfeit coin/currency/stamps, forged documents, false seals, obscene objects, and the tools to make any of these). The authorised officer can enter, search, seize, safely convey the goods, and — importantly — also arrest anyone found there who appears complicit with the requisite guilty knowledge.
essential_elements: Issuing authority limited to DM, Sub-divisional Magistrate, or first-class Magistrate, and requires information plus such inquiry as the Magistrate thinks necessary.
The warrant authorises a police officer above constable rank to enter, search, seize, and safely dispose of the suspected items.
It also authorises arresting persons found at the place who appear privy to the deposit/sale/production, with knowledge or reasonable cause to suspect the item's stolen/objectionable character.
'Objectionable articles' is an exhaustively defined list — the section doesn't apply to items outside that list.
breakdown.how_to_read: The arrest power under clause (e) is bundled into a search-warrant provision — an unusual combination worth flagging when scrutinising the legality of any arrest made during execution of a Section 97 warrant, since it depends on the person's apparent complicity and guilty knowledge, not merely presence at the scene.

sections.title: Power to declare certain publications forfeited and to issue search-warrants for same
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where—
(a) any newspaper, or book; or
(b) any document,
wherever printed, appears to the State Government to contain any matter the publication of which is punishable under section 152 or section 196 or section 197 or section 294 or section 295 or section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (45 of 2023), the State Government may, by notification, stating the grounds of its opinion, declare every copy of the issue of the newspaper containing such matter, and every copy of such book or other document to be forfeited to Government, and thereupon any police officer may seize the same wherever found in India and any Magistrate may by warrant authorise any police officer not below the rank of sub-inspector to enter upon and search for the same in any premises where any copy of such issue, or any such book or other document may be or may be reasonably suspected to be.
(2) In this section and in section 99—
(a) "newspaper" and "book" have the same meanings as in the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867 (25 of 1867);
(b) "document" includes any painting, drawing or photograph, or other visible representation.
(3) No order passed or action taken under this section shall be called in question in any Court otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of section 99.

breakdown.plain_summary: A press-control power: where a newspaper, book, or document appears to the State Government to contain matter punishable under specific serious offences (sedition-adjacent, promoting enmity, obscenity, etc., under the BNS), it may declare all copies forfeited by a reasoned notification, triggering nationwide seizure and search authority. This is a significant restriction on publication — which is precisely why Section 99 immediately provides a High Court challenge route, and sub-section (3) makes that the EXCLUSIVE way to question such an order.
essential_elements: Trigger: State Government's opinion that the publication is punishable under one of the specifically listed BNS sections.
Mechanism: a reasoned notification declaring every copy forfeited to Government.
Effect: nationwide seizure power for any police officer, plus Magistrate-authorised search power for sub-inspector-rank-or-above officers.
'Document' is broadly defined to include paintings, drawings, photographs, and other visible representations, not just text.
Sub-section (3) makes Section 99 the EXCLUSIVE remedy — no other Court challenge route is available.
breakdown.how_to_read: Because sub-section (3) forecloses any other mode of challenge, always route a forfeiture challenge specifically through the Section 99 High Court Special Bench application — a writ petition or other proceeding attacking the same order on the same grounds is liable to be treated as barred.

sections.title: Application to High Court to set aside declaration of forfeiture
sections.raw_text:
(1) Any person having any interest in any newspaper, book or other document, in respect of which a declaration of forfeiture has been made under section 98, may, within two months from the date of publication in the Official Gazette of such declaration, apply to the High Court to set aside such declaration on the ground that the issue of the newspaper, or the book or other document, in respect of which the declaration was made, did not contain any such matter as is referred to in sub-section (1) of section 98.
(2) Every such application shall, where the High Court consists of three or more Judges, be heard and determined by a Special Bench of the High Court composed of three Judges and where the High Court consists of less than three Judges, such Special Bench shall be composed of all the Judges of that High Court.
(3) On the hearing of any such application with reference to any newspaper, any copy of such newspaper may be given in evidence in aid of the proof of the nature or tendency of the words, signs or visible representations contained in such newspaper, in respect of which the declaration of forfeiture was made.
(4) The High Court shall, if it is not satisfied that the issue of the newspaper, or the book or other document, in respect of which the application has been made, contained any such matter as is referred to in sub-section (1) of section 98, set aside the declaration of forfeiture.
(5) Where there is a difference of opinion among the Judges forming the Special Bench, the decision shall be in accordance with the opinion of the majority of those Judges.

breakdown.plain_summary: The dedicated remedy for a Section 98 forfeiture: any interested person has 2 months from Gazette publication to apply to the High Court, which must hear it through a specially constituted 3-Judge Bench (or all Judges, if the High Court has fewer than three) — a deliberately weighty forum reflecting the seriousness of press-forfeiture orders. The Court sets aside the forfeiture unless satisfied the publication genuinely contained the offending matter; majority opinion governs any disagreement among the Bench.
essential_elements: Standing: any person with an interest in the forfeited newspaper/book/document.
Limitation: 2 months from the date of Official Gazette publication of the declaration.
Mandatory Special Bench of 3 Judges (or the full High Court if it has fewer than three Judges) — not a single Judge or ordinary Division Bench.
Burden effectively favours the applicant: forfeiture is set aside unless the High Court IS satisfied the offending matter was genuinely present.
Majority opinion governs Bench disagreements.
breakdown.how_to_read: The 2-month limitation period is strict and runs from Gazette publication, not from when the affected person actually learns of the forfeiture — advise clients to monitor the Official Gazette proactively if a forfeiture notification is anticipated.

sections.title: Search for persons wrongfully confined
sections.raw_text: If any District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or Magistrate of the first class has reason to believe that any person is confined under such circumstances that the confinement amounts to an offence, he may issue a search-warrant, and the person to whom such warrant is directed may search for the person so confined; and such search shall be made in accordance therewith, and the person, if found, shall be immediately taken before a Magistrate, who shall make such order as in the circumstances of the case seems proper.

breakdown.plain_summary: A rescue-oriented search-warrant power distinct from property searches: where a Magistrate believes someone is being unlawfully confined (kidnapping, illegal detention, etc.), a search-warrant can be issued specifically to locate and recover that person, who must then be immediately produced before a Magistrate for appropriate orders.
essential_elements: Issuing authority: DM, Sub-divisional Magistrate, or first-class Magistrate.
Trigger: reason to believe confinement amounting to an offence.
The recovered person must be taken immediately before a Magistrate, who then makes whatever order the circumstances warrant.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the primary statutory search tool in kidnapping/illegal-confinement cases where the victim's location is suspected but not yet confirmed — distinct from, and complementary to, the specific abducted-female power in Section 101.

sections.title: Power to compel restoration of abducted females
sections.raw_text: Upon complaint made on oath of the abduction or unlawful detention of a woman, or a female child for any unlawful purpose, a District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or Magistrate of the first class may make an order for the immediate restoration of such woman to her liberty, or of such female child to her parent, guardian or other person having the lawful charge of such child, and may compel compliance with such order, using such force as may be necessary.

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes Part A/B's specialised-search provisions. A sworn complaint of a woman's or female child's abduction/unlawful detention for an unlawful purpose empowers a senior Magistrate to directly order restoration — a woman to her own liberty, a child to whoever lawfully has charge of her — with force authorised as necessary to enforce that order.
essential_elements: Trigger: a complaint made ON OATH of abduction or unlawful detention for an unlawful purpose.
Two distinct restoration outcomes: restoration of a woman to her own liberty, or of a female child to her parent/guardian/lawful custodian.
The Magistrate may use necessary force to compel compliance with the restoration order.
breakdown.how_to_read: Unlike Section 100's search-and-produce mechanism, this section empowers a direct restoration ORDER on the strength of a sworn complaint — a faster, more targeted remedy specifically for abduction/unlawful-detention cases involving women and female children.

sections.title: Direction, etc., of search-warrants
sections.raw_text: The provisions of sections 32, 72, 74, 76, 79, 80 and 81 shall, so far as may be, apply to all search-warrants issued under section 96, section 97, section 98 or section 100.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Part C (General provisions relating to searches). Rather than repeating the mechanics, this section cross-applies the arrest-warrant machinery (aid to persons executing a warrant, form/duration, who a warrant may be directed to, territorial reach, and cross-jurisdiction execution) to every search-warrant issued under Sections 96, 97, 98, or 100.
essential_elements: Applies specifically to search-warrants under Sections 96, 97, 98, and 100 (not every search-related provision in the Chapter).
Imports Sections 32, 72, 74, 76, 79, 80, and 81 'so far as may be' — with necessary adaptation for search rather than arrest context.
breakdown.how_to_read: When challenging a search-warrant's execution mechanics (form, direction, cross-district execution), check the corresponding arrest-warrant provision imported by this section — the same standards apply by cross-reference.

sections.title: Persons in charge of closed place to allow search
sections.raw_text:
(1) Whenever any place liable to search or inspection under this Chapter is closed, any person residing in, or being in charge of, such place, shall, on demand of the officer or other person executing the warrant, and on production of the warrant, allow him free ingress thereto, and afford all reasonable facilities for a search therein.
(2) If ingress into such place cannot be so obtained, the officer or other person executing the warrant may proceed in the manner provided by sub-section (2) of section 44.
(3) Where any person in or about such place is reasonably suspected of concealing about his person any article for which search should be made, such person may be searched and if such person is a woman, the search shall be made by another woman with strict regard to decency.
(4) Before making a search under this Chapter, the officer or other person about to make it shall call upon two or more independent and respectable inhabitants of the locality in which the place to be searched is situate or of any other locality if no such inhabitant of the said locality is available or is willing to be a witness to the search, to attend and witness the search and may issue an order in writing to them or any of them so to do.
(5) The search shall be made in their presence, and a list of all things seized in the course of such search and of the places in which they are respectively found shall be prepared by such officer or other person and signed by such witnesses; but no person witnessing a search under this section shall be required to attend the Court as a witness of the search unless specially summoned by it.
(6) The occupant of the place searched, or some person in his behalf, shall, in every instance, be permitted to attend during the search, and a copy of the list prepared under this section, signed by the said witnesses, shall be delivered to such occupant or person.
(7) When any person is searched under sub-section (3), a list of all things taken possession of shall be prepared, and a copy thereof shall be delivered to such person.
(8) Any person who, without reasonable cause, refuses or neglects to attend and witness a search under this section, when called upon to do so by an order in writing delivered or tendered to him, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under section 222 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (45 of 2023).

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the core procedural discipline for how a search must actually be conducted — the statutory basis for the familiar 'panchnama' practice. Occupants must permit free entry on demand and warrant production; forced entry follows Section 44's procedure if refused. Two or more independent, respectable local witnesses must attend and sign the seizure list. The occupant may attend throughout and gets a copy of the list. Personal searches of suspected persons follow the same female-searched-by-female safeguard seen elsewhere. Refusing to witness a search without reasonable cause is itself made an offence.
essential_elements: Occupant's duty: allow free ingress and reasonable search facilities on demand and warrant production.
Forced-entry fallback: Section 44(2) procedure if ingress is refused.
Personal search of a suspected person present: permitted, with the female-searched-by-female rule for women.
Mandatory: two or more independent, respectable local witnesses (or from elsewhere, if none locally available/willing) to attend and sign the seizure list.
Witnesses need not personally testify in Court unless specially summoned.
The occupant may attend throughout and must receive a signed copy of the seizure list.
Refusal to witness a search without reasonable cause is an offence under BNS Section 222.
