breakdown.how_to_read: Non-compliance with the independent-witness requirement is one of the most frequently litigated search-and-seizure defects — always check whether the witnesses were genuinely independent and local (or a documented reason exists for using outsiders) before accepting a seizure list as reliable.

sections.title: Disposal of things found in search beyond jurisdiction
sections.raw_text: When, in the execution of a search-warrant at any place beyond the local jurisdiction of the Court which issued the same, any of the things for which search is made, are found, such things, together with the list of the same prepared under the provisions hereinafter contained, shall be immediately taken before the Court issuing the warrant, unless such place is nearer to the Magistrate having jurisdiction therein than to such Court, in which case the list and things shall be immediately taken before such Magistrate; and, unless there be good cause to the contrary, such Magistrate shall make an order authorising them to be taken to such Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: A routing rule for items seized outside the issuing Court's own territory: ordinarily they go straight back to the issuing Court, but if the local jurisdictional Magistrate is actually closer than the issuing Court, the items go there first, with that Magistrate then ordering onward transmission to the issuing Court (absent good cause not to).
essential_elements: Default: items and seizure list go directly to the issuing Court.
Proximity exception: if the local Magistrate's jurisdiction is nearer than the issuing Court, items go there first.
That local Magistrate must order onward transmission to the issuing Court, unless good cause exists not to.
breakdown.how_to_read: A practical logistics rule — challenge any unexplained delay in transmission under this section as a possible break in the chain of custody, particularly where the 'nearer Magistrate' route was used but no subsequent transmission order appears on record.

sections.title: Recording of search and seizure through audio-video electronic means
sections.raw_text: The process of conducting search of a place or taking possession of any property, article or thing under this Chapter or under section 185, including preparation of the list of all things seized in the course of such search and seizure and signing of such list by witnesses, shall be recorded through any audio-video electronic means preferably mobile phone and the police officer shall without delay forward such recording to the District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class.

breakdown.plain_summary: Opens Part D (Miscellaneous) with a landmark BNSS-specific transparency reform: every search and seizure under this Chapter (or under Section 185's investigation-search power) — including preparation and witness-signing of the seizure list — must now be video-recorded, preferably on a mobile phone, with the recording promptly sent to a Magistrate. This did not exist under the old CrPC and is designed to curb planted evidence and coerced or fabricated panchnamas.
essential_elements: Mandatory recording covers the entire search/seizure process, including list preparation and witness signing — not just the initial entry.
'Mobile phone' is stated as the preferred (not exclusive) recording device — any audio-video electronic means suffices.
The recording must be forwarded WITHOUT DELAY to a DM, Sub-divisional Magistrate, or first-class Judicial Magistrate.
Applies to searches under this Chapter and also under Section 185 (police investigation search power).
breakdown.how_to_read: This is one of the most significant new evidentiary safeguards in the BNSS — the absence of a video recording, or an unexplained delay in forwarding it to the Magistrate, is now a strong and specific ground to challenge the integrity of a search/seizure, distinct from the older independent-witness safeguard in Section 103.

sections.title: Power of police officer to seize certain property
sections.raw_text:
(1) Any police officer may seize any property which may be alleged or suspected to have been stolen, or which may be found under circumstances which create suspicion of the commission of any offence.
(2) Such police officer, if subordinate to the officer in charge of a police station, shall forthwith report the seizure to that officer.
(3) Every police officer acting under sub-section (1) shall forthwith report the seizure to the Magistrate having jurisdiction and where the property seized is such that it cannot be conveniently transported to the Court, or where there is difficulty in securing proper accommodation for the custody of such property, or where the continued retention of the property in police custody may not be considered necessary for the purpose of investigation, he may give custody thereof to any person on his executing a bond undertaking to produce the property before the Court as and when required and to give effect to the further orders of the Court as to the disposal of the same:
Provided that where the property seized under sub-section (1) is subject to speedy and natural decay and if the person entitled to the possession of such property is unknown or absent and the value of such property is less than five hundred rupees, it may forthwith be sold by auction under the orders of the Superintendent of Police and the provisions of sections 503 and 504 shall, as nearly as may be practicable, apply to the net proceeds of such sale.

breakdown.plain_summary: A general, warrant-free seizure power (independent of any search-warrant) for property suspected stolen or otherwise suspicious. Two reporting duties follow: up the chain to the station officer (if the seizing officer is subordinate), and to the jurisdictional Magistrate. Where practical custody is difficult or unnecessary for the investigation, the property can be released to a custodian on a bond to produce it on demand. A narrow auction exception applies for low-value (under Rs. 500), perishable, unclaimed property.
essential_elements: No warrant is required — this is an independent, general seizure power based on suspicion alone.
Dual reporting: to the officer in charge of the station (if the seizing officer is subordinate) and to the jurisdictional Magistrate, both 'forthwith.'
Custody alternative: release to a bonded custodian where transport/accommodation is difficult or continued police custody isn't investigatively necessary.
Narrow auction exception: perishable property, unknown/absent claimant, and value under Rs. 500 — sold under Superintendent of Police orders, with Sections 503-504 governing the sale proceeds.
breakdown.how_to_read: The bonded-custodian release mechanism is a practical tool to avoid property languishing indefinitely in police malkhanas — where seized property (e.g., a vehicle) sits unreleased despite no clear investigative need for continued custody, this sub-section (3) mechanism is the basis to press for interim release.

sections.title: Attachment, forfeiture or restoration of property
sections.raw_text:
(1) Where a police officer making an investigation has reason to believe that any property is derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, as a result of a criminal activity or from the commission of any offence, he may, with the approval of the Superintendent of Police or Commissioner of Police, make an application to the Court or the Magistrate exercising jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence or commit for trial or try the case, for the attachment of such property.
(2) If the Court or the Magistrate has reasons to believe, whether before or after taking evidence, that all or any of such properties are proceeds of crime, the Court or the Magistrate may issue a notice upon such person calling upon him to show cause within a period of fourteen days as to why an order of attachment shall not be made.
(3) Where the notice issued to any person under sub-section (2) specifies any property as being held by any other person on behalf of such person, a copy of the notice shall also be served upon such other person.
(4) The Court or the Magistrate may, after considering the explanation, if any, to the show-cause notice issued under sub-section (2) and the material fact available before such Court or Magistrate and after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to such person or persons, may pass an order of attachment, in respect of those properties which are found to be the proceeds of crime:
Provided that if such person does not appear before the Court or the Magistrate or represent his case before the Court or Magistrate within a period of fourteen days specified in the show-cause notice, the Court or the Magistrate may proceed to pass the ex parte order.
(5) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (2), if the Court or the Magistrate is of the opinion that issuance of notice under the said sub-section would defeat the object of attachment or seizure, the Court or Magistrate may by an interim order passed ex parte direct attachment or seizure of such property, and such order shall remain in force till an order under sub-section (6) is passed.
(6) If the Court or the Magistrate finds the attached or seized properties to be the proceeds of crime, the Court or the Magistrate shall by order direct the District Magistrate to rateably distribute such proceeds of crime to the persons who are affected by such crime.
(7) On receipt of an order passed under sub-section (6), the District Magistrate shall, within a period of sixty days distribute the proceeds of crime either by himself or authorise any officer subordinate to him to effect such distribution.
(8) If there are no claimants to receive such proceeds or no claimant is ascertainable or there is any surplus after satisfying the claimants, such proceeds of crime shall stand forfeited to the Government.

breakdown.plain_summary: One of the BNSS's genuinely new tools, borrowed conceptually from anti-money-laundering practice (like PMLA): investigating officers can seek attachment of 'proceeds of crime' — property derived from criminal activity — with senior police approval, through the trial Court/Magistrate. A show-cause notice with a 14-day response window is the default, but if notice itself would defeat the purpose (e.g., tip off the person to dissipate assets), an ex parte interim attachment/seizure order can be made immediately. Once confirmed as proceeds of crime, the District Magistrate must distribute the property to victims within 60 days, with any surplus or unclaimed portion forfeited to Government — meaning this mechanism is oriented towards victim compensation, not just punitive confiscation.
essential_elements: Application requires senior police approval (SP or Commissioner of Police) before being made to the trial Court/Magistrate.
Default process: 14-day show-cause notice, with notice also served on any third party holding the property on the suspect's behalf.
Ex parte final order is available if the person doesn't appear/respond within the 14 days.

Ex parte INTERIM attachment/seizure (bypassing notice altogether) is available where notice itself would defeat the attachment's purpose — but this interim order only lasts until the final sub-section (6) order.
Confirmed proceeds of crime must be rateably distributed to crime-affected persons by the District Magistrate within 60 days of the order.
Unclaimed or surplus proceeds are forfeited to Government.
breakdown.how_to_read: This victim-compensation-oriented forfeiture mechanism is a genuinely new feature not present in the old CrPC — practitioners representing victims of property-related offences (fraud, cheating, theft rings) should actively consider invoking Section 107 alongside the underlying prosecution to secure compensation through the rateable-distribution mechanism, rather than relying solely on compensation orders at sentencing.

sections.title: Magistrate may direct search in his presence
sections.raw_text: Any Magistrate may direct a search to be made in his presence of any place for the search of which he is competent to issue a search-warrant.

breakdown.plain_summary: A short but useful provision: rather than delegating a search entirely to police, a Magistrate can personally direct and be present for a search of any place within their own search-warrant-issuing competence — a hands-on oversight option.
essential_elements: The Magistrate's power to direct an in-presence search is coextensive with their competence to issue a search-warrant for that place in the first place.
breakdown.how_to_read: A Magistrate-supervised search is a strong safeguard where the integrity of a search is likely to be contested — practitioners can request this route in sensitive cases to pre-empt later procedural challenges.

sections.title: Power to impound document, etc., produced
sections.raw_text: Any Court may, if it thinks fit, impound any document or thing produced before it under this Sanhita.

breakdown.plain_summary: Closes Chapter VII. A simple, discretionary power: once any document or thing is produced before a Court under the Sanhita (by whatever mechanism — summons, search-warrant, voluntary production), the Court may impound (retain custody of) it if it thinks fit.
essential_elements: Applies to any document/thing already produced before the Court, regardless of the production mechanism.
Purely discretionary ('if it thinks fit') — no specific precondition is prescribed.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the Court's general custody-retention power over exhibits and produced material — relevant whenever a party seeks the return of a document/item the Court has chosen to impound rather than release.

sections.title: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes
sections.raw_text:
110. Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes.—(1) Where a Court in the territories to which this Sanhita extends (hereafter in this section referred to as the said territories) desires that—
        (a) a summons to an accused person; or
        (b) a warrant for the arrest of an accused person; or
        (c) a summons to any person requiring him to attend and produce a document or other thing, or to produce it; or
        (d) a search-warrant,
issued by it shall be served or executed at any place,—
        (i) within the local jurisdiction of a Court in any State or area in India outside the said territories, it may send such summons or warrant in duplicate by post or otherwise, to the presiding officer of that Court to be served or executed; and where any summons referred to in clause (a) or clause (c) has been so served, the provisions of section 70 shall apply in relation to such summons as if the presiding officer of the Court to whom it is sent were a Magistrate in the said territories;
        (ii) in any country or place outside India in respect of which arrangements have been made by the Central Government with the Government of such country or place for service or execution of summons or warrant in relation to criminal matters (hereafter in this section referred to as the contracting State), it may send such summons or warrant in duplicate in such form, directed to such Court, Judge or Magistrate, and send to such authority for transmission, as the Central Government may, by notification, specify in this behalf.
    (2) Where a Court in the said territories has received for service or execution—
        (a) a summons to an accused person; or
        (b) a warrant for the arrest of an accused person; or
        (c) a summons to any person requiring him to attend and produce a document or other thing, or to produce it; or
        (d) a search-warrant,
issued by—
        (I) a Court in any State or area in India outside the said territories;
        (II) a Court, Judge or Magistrate in a contracting State,
it shall cause the same to be served or executed as if it were a summons or warrant received by it from another Court in the said territories for service or execution within its local jurisdiction; and where—
        (i) a warrant of arrest has been executed, the person arrested shall, so far as possible, be dealt with in accordance with the procedure specified by sections 82 and 83;
        (ii) a search-warrant has been executed, the things found in the search shall, so far as possible, be dealt with in accordance with the procedure specified by section 104:
    Provided that in a case where a summons or search-warrant received from a contracting State has been executed, the documents or things produced or things found in the search shall be forwarded to the Court issuing the summons or search-warrant through such authority as the Central Government may, by notification, specify in this behalf.

breakdown.plain_summary:
This is the master switch that makes India's criminal process machinery (summons, arrest warrants, production summons, search-warrants) work across borders — both internal (between Indian States) and external (with foreign "contracting States"). It has two halves: outbound (an Indian Court wants its own process served elsewhere) and inbound (an Indian Court is asked to serve someone else's process here).

Outbound: if the target is in another Indian State, the Court simply posts the process in duplicate to the presiding officer there for service/execution, and the ordinary "return of service" rule (Section 70) applies as if that officer were a local Magistrate. If the target is in a contracting State (a country with a reciprocal arrangement with India), the process goes in duplicate, in the prescribed form, through the Central Government's designated transmission channel.

Inbound: whether the process arrives from another Indian State or from a contracting State's Court/Judge/Magistrate, the receiving Indian Court treats it exactly like a domestic warrant/summons from a sister Court — same execution procedure. An executed arrest warrant follows the ordinary "arrested-outside-district" rules (Sections 82-83); an executed search-warrant follows the ordinary disposal-of-seized-things rule (Section 104). The one twist for foreign-originated process: seized documents/things go back to the requesting foreign Court only through the Central Government's designated channel, not directly.
essential_elements: Covers four process types: accused-person summons, arrest warrant, document-production summons, and search-warrant.
Outbound to another Indian State: sent in duplicate by post (or otherwise) to that State's presiding officer.
Outbound to a contracting State: sent in duplicate, in prescribed form, through the Central Government's notified transmission authority.
Inbound process (domestic or foreign) is executed by the receiving Court exactly as if it were a domestic warrant/summons.
Foreign-executed search results are routed back only through the Central-Government-notified authority, not directly to the foreign Court.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A 'contracting State' only exists where the Central Government has actually made reciprocal arrangements with that country's government — there is no automatic right to send process abroad without such an arrangement.
The special return-channel proviso (routing seized material back through the notified authority) applies only to process received from a contracting State, not to inter-State domestic process.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as the general gateway section before Chapter VIII proper begins — it establishes that summons/warrants/search-warrants are not confined by State or national borders once the reciprocal machinery is switched on. Pair sub-section (1) (outbound) with sub-section (2) (inbound) as mirror images of the same transmission pipeline.

sections.title: Definitions

breakdown.plain_summary: Chapter VIII's own dictionary. These five definitions are deliberately broad and PMLA-flavoured: "property" sweeps in every kind of asset (movable, immovable, tangible, intangible, and even the paperwork that proves title to it); "proceeds of crime" covers anything derived from criminal activity, directly or indirectly, including its money value if the actual asset is gone or mixed with other funds; "identifying" and "tracing" describe the investigative work of proving an asset's criminal origin and following its trail through transfers.
essential_elements: 'Contracting State' requires an actual treaty or arrangement between the Central Government and that country's government.
'Proceeds of crime' includes both the property itself and its money value — useful where the original asset has been spent, converted, or laundered.
'Property' is defined exhaustively wide: corporeal/incorporeal, movable/immovable, tangible/intangible, plus title documents.
'Identifying' = proving criminal derivation/use; 'tracing' = following nature, source, movement, title, and ownership.
exceptions_and_qualifications: These definitions apply only 'in this Chapter' (Chapter VIII) unless context otherwise requires — they don't automatically govern the rest of the Sanhita.
breakdown.how_to_read: Keep this section open as a reference while reading Sections 115-122 — nearly every substantive attachment/forfeiture provision that follows leans on these five terms, especially 'proceeds of crime' and 'property'.

sections.title: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India
sections.raw_text:
112. Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India.—(1) If, in the course of an investigation into an offence, an application is made by the investigating officer or any officer superior in rank to the investigating officer that evidence may be available in a country or place outside India, any Criminal Court may issue a letter of request to a Court or an authority in that country or place competent to deal with such request to examine orally any person supposed to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case and to record his statement made in the course of such examination and also to require such person or any other person to produce any document or thing which may be in his possession pertaining to the case and to forward all the evidence so taken or collected or the authenticated copies thereof or the thing so collected to the Court issuing such letter.
    (2) The letter of request shall be transmitted in such manner as the Central Government may specify in this behalf.
    (3) Every statement recorded or document or thing received under sub-section (1) shall be deemed to be the evidence collected during the course of investigation under this Sanhita.

breakdown.plain_summary: When evidence needed for an Indian investigation is sitting in another country, an Indian Criminal Court can issue a "letter of request" (sometimes called a letter rogatory) to that country's competent authority, asking it to examine a witness on oath, record their statement, and collect any relevant documents or things, then send everything back. The request is triggered by an application from the investigating officer (or someone senior to them) — the Court doesn't act on its own initiative. Crucially, whatever comes back — statements, documents, things — is deemed to be evidence collected during the Indian investigation itself, giving it full evidentiary standing under the Sanhita without needing a fresh domestic re-collection step.
essential_elements: Trigger: an application by the investigating officer, or an officer superior in rank to them, in the course of an investigation.
The Criminal Court issues the letter of request to a competent Court/authority in the foreign country or place.
Scope of the request: oral examination on oath, recording of statement, and production of documents/things.
Transmission method is as specified by the Central Government.
Legal effect: evidence so obtained is deemed evidence collected during the domestic investigation under the Sanhita.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is an outbound request only — India asking a foreign authority for help; the inbound mirror is Section 113.
The provision only operates where the foreign country/place has a competent Court or authority willing/able to act on the request; there's no compulsion mechanism over a foreign sovereign.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside Section 113, its exact mirror image for inbound requests. The 'deemed evidence' clause in sub-section (3) is the practical payoff — it saves the prosecution from having to separately prove foreign-collected material meets domestic evidentiary formalities.

sections.title: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India
sections.raw_text:
113. Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India.—(1) Upon receipt of a letter of request from a Court or an authority in a country or place outside India competent to issue such letter in that country or place for the examination of any person or production of any document or thing in relation to an offence under investigation in that country or place, the Central Government may, if it thinks fit—
        (i) forward the same to the Chief Judicial Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate as he may appoint in this behalf, who shall thereupon summon the person before him and record his statement or cause the document or thing to be produced; or
        (ii) send the letter to any police officer for investigation, who shall thereupon investigate into the offence in the same manner,
as if the offence had been committed within India.
    (2) All the evidence taken or collected under sub-section (1), or authenticated copies thereof or the thing so collected, shall be forwarded by the Magistrate or police officer, as the case may be, to the Central Government for transmission to the Court or the authority issuing the letter of request, in such manner as the Central Government may deem fit.

breakdown.plain_summary: The inbound mirror of Section 112: when a foreign Court or competent authority sends India a letter of request for help investigating an offence committed abroad, the Central Government has discretion (not obligation — "may, if it thinks fit") to route the request one of two ways: to a Chief Judicial Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate nominated by them, who summons the person and records the statement or has the document/thing produced; or to a police officer, who investigates the underlying offence exactly as if it had happened in India. Either way, everything collected is funnelled back to the Central Government for onward transmission to the requesting foreign authority.
essential_elements: Trigger: receipt of a letter of request from a competent foreign Court/authority regarding an offence under investigation abroad.
The Central Government has discretion whether to act on it at all ('if it thinks fit').
Two execution routes: (i) via a Chief/Judicial Magistrate who examines the person or secures the document/thing, or (ii) via a police officer who investigates the offence as if committed in India.
All evidence collected is forwarded to the Central Government, which transmits it onward to the requesting foreign Court/authority.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Central Government's discretion means a foreign request can be declined; there's no automatic entitlement to Indian assistance.

The investigation proceeds 'as if the offence had been committed within India' — Indian procedural safeguards and standards govern the domestic collection process even though the underlying offence is foreign.
breakdown.how_to_read: Compare directly against Section 112 — same mechanism, opposite direction. The Central Government is the clearinghouse in both directions, which is the throughline for all of Chapter VIII's international-cooperation provisions.

sections.title: Assistance in securing transfer of persons
sections.raw_text:
114. Assistance in securing transfer of persons.—(1) Where a Court in India, in relation to a criminal matter, desires that a warrant for arrest of any person to attend or produce a document or other thing issued by it shall be executed in any place in a contracting State, it shall send such warrant in duplicate in such form to such Court, Judge or Magistrate through such authority, as the Central Government may, by notification, specify in this behalf and that Court, Judge or Magistrate, as the case may be, shall cause the same to be executed.
    (2) If, in the course of an investigation or any inquiry into an offence, an application is made by the investigating officer or any officer superior in rank to the investigating officer that the attendance of a person who is in any place in a contracting State is required in connection with such investigation or inquiry and the Court is satisfied that such attendance is so required, it shall issue a summons or warrant, in duplicate, against the said person to such Court, Judge or Magistrate, in such form as the Central Government may, by notification, specify in this behalf, to cause the same to be served or executed.
    (3) Where a Court in India, in relation to a criminal matter, has received a warrant for arrest of any person requiring him to attend or attend and produce a document or other thing in that Court or before any other investigating agency, issued by a Court, Judge or Magistrate in a contracting State, the same shall be executed as if it is the warrant received by it from another Court in India for execution within its local limits.
    (4) Where a person transferred to a contracting State pursuant to sub-section (3) is a prisoner in India, the Court in India or the Central Government may impose such conditions as that Court or Government deems fit.
    (5) Where the person transferred to India pursuant to sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) is a prisoner in a contracting State, the Court in India shall ensure that the conditions subject to which the prisoner is transferred to India are complied with and such prisoner shall be kept in such custody subject to such conditions as the Central Government may direct in writing.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section lets Indian Courts get a person physically brought over (or sent over) for a criminal matter, when that person is in a contracting State — including where that person happens to be a prisoner there or here. Outbound (sub-sections 1-2): an Indian Court sends an arrest warrant, or a summons/warrant application triggered by the investigating officer, to the foreign Court through the Central-Government-notified channel, for execution abroad. Inbound (sub-section 3): a warrant arriving from a contracting State's Court is executed here exactly like a domestic warrant from another Indian Court. The prisoner-specific safeguards (sub-sections 4-5) protect custodial status on both ends: if an Indian prisoner is being sent abroad, the Indian Court/Central Government can attach conditions; if a foreign prisoner is being brought into India, the Indian Court must ensure the transfer conditions set are honoured and keep that person in custody on the terms the Central Government directs.
essential_elements: Outbound arrest-warrant execution abroad: sent in duplicate, in prescribed form, through the Central-Government-notified authority.
Outbound summons/warrant triggered by an investigating officer's (or a superior's) application, where the Court is satisfied attendance is required.
Inbound warrant from a contracting State is executed exactly as a domestic inter-Court warrant.
Special conditions attach when the person being transferred (in either direction) is already a prisoner.
Custody of a foreign prisoner transferred into India is governed by Central Government directions.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Only operates with a genuine contracting State — no reciprocal arrangement, no mechanism.
Prisoner-transfer conditions are set at the discretion of the Court/Central Government, not fixed by the statute itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the parallel structure: sub-sections (1)-(2) mirror Section 110's outbound logic but specifically for compelling a person's attendance/production; sub-section (3) mirrors the inbound logic; sub-sections (4)-(5) are the added prisoner-custody layer unique to this section.

sections.title: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property
sections.raw_text:
115. Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property.—(1) Where a Court in India has reasonable grounds to believe that any property obtained by any person is derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, by such person from the commission of an offence, it may make an order of attachment or forfeiture of such property, as it may deem fit under the provisions of sections 116 to 122 (both inclusive).
    (2) Where the Court has made an order for attachment or forfeiture of any property under sub-section (1), and such property is suspected to be in a contracting State, the Court may issue a letter of request to a Court or an authority in the contracting State for execution of such order.
    (3) Where a letter of request is received by the Central Government from a Court or an authority in a contracting State requesting attachment or forfeiture of the property in India, derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, by any person from the commission of an offence committed in that contracting State, the Central Government may forward such letter of request to the Court, as it thinks fit, for execution in accordance with the provisions of sections 116 to 122 (both inclusive) or, as the case may be, any other law for the time being in force.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the opening section of the property-attachment-and-forfeiture machinery that runs through Section 122. It empowers an Indian Court, on reasonable grounds that a person's property is criminally derived, to order attachment or forfeiture under the detailed procedure in Sections 116-122. It then extends this outward and inward: if the suspect property is believed to be sitting in a contracting State, the Indian Court can request that State's Court/authority to execute the order there; conversely, if a contracting State asks India (via the Central Government) to attach or forfeit crime-derived property located in India, the Central Government forwards that request to an Indian Court to execute using the same Sections 116-122 procedure (or any other applicable law).
essential_elements: Threshold: 'reasonable grounds to believe' the property is derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, from an offence.
The Court's order of attachment or forfeiture is made under, and must follow, the detailed procedure in Sections 116-122.
Outbound: property suspected to be in a contracting State — letter of request to that State's Court/authority for execution.
Inbound: a contracting State's letter of request for India-located property is forwarded by the Central Government to an Indian Court for execution.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The inbound route can also proceed under 'any other law for the time being in force' if Sections 116-122 don't fit — an express flexibility valve.
This is a civil-in-character forfeiture mechanism (property-focused), distinct from a criminal conviction — it runs on its own procedural track.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as the umbrella/trigger section; Sections 116-122 are the operative machinery it points to. Read them together as one continuous procedure: identify (116) → seize/attach (117) → manage (118) → notice (119) → forfeit (120) → fine-in-lieu option (121) → anti-evasion (122).

sections.title: Identifying unlawfully acquired property
sections.raw_text:
116. Identifying unlawfully acquired property.—(1) The Court shall, under sub-section (1), or on receipt of a letter of request under sub-section (3) of section 115, direct any police officer not below the rank of Sub-Inspector of Police to take all steps necessary for tracing and identifying such property.
    (2) The steps referred to in sub-section (1) may include any inquiry, investigation or survey in respect of any person, place, property, assets, documents, books of account in any bank or public financial institutions or any other relevant matters.
    (3) Any inquiry, investigation or survey referred to in sub-section (2) shall be carried out by an officer mentioned in sub-section (1) in accordance with such directions issued by the said Court in this behalf.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once a Court decides property may be crime-derived (under Section 115(1), or on a foreign letter of request under Section 115(3)), it directs a police officer of at least Sub-Inspector rank to actually go trace and identify that property. The investigative toolkit is deliberately broad — inquiry, investigation, or survey of any person, place, property, assets, documents, or bank/financial-institution records — but it is not free-ranging; it must follow the Court's own directions.
essential_elements: Minimum rank for the directed officer: Sub-Inspector of Police.
Triggers: a Section 115(1) domestic finding, or a Section 115(3) foreign letter of request.
Permitted investigative steps: inquiry, investigation, or survey — of persons, places, property, assets, documents, and bank/financial-institution records.
All such steps must be carried out in accordance with the directions issued by the Court.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The officer's investigative reach into bank and financial-institution records is expressly authorised here — a specific carve-out that would otherwise raise confidentiality questions.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is step one of the Sections 116-122 chain — pure fact-finding, no seizure yet. Seizure/attachment power comes next, in Section 117.

sections.title: Seizure or attachment of property
sections.raw_text:
117. Seizure or attachment of property.—(1) Where any officer conducting an inquiry or investigation under section 116 has a reason to believe that any property in relation to which such inquiry or investigation is being conducted is likely to be concealed, transferred or dealt with in any manner which will result in disposal of such property, he may make an order for seizing such property and where it is not practicable to seize such property, he may make an order of attachment directing that such property shall not be transferred or otherwise dealt with, except with the prior permission of the officer making such order, and a copy of such order shall be served on the person concerned.
    (2) Any order made under sub-section (1) shall have no effect unless the said order is confirmed by an order of the said Court, within a period of thirty days of its being made.

breakdown.plain_summary: Gives the investigating officer emergency power to freeze suspect property before it disappears. If the officer, while conducting the Section 116 inquiry, has reason to believe the property is at risk of being concealed, transferred, or otherwise disposed of, they can seize it outright; where seizure isn't practical (e.g., immovable property or a bank account), they can instead order attachment — freezing further dealing with the property without the officer's prior permission — and must serve a copy of that order on the person concerned. Critically, this is only a provisional, officer-level power: it automatically lapses unless the Court confirms it within thirty days.
essential_elements: Threshold: 'reason to believe' the property is likely to be concealed, transferred, or disposed of.
Two available measures: outright seizure, or (where seizure isn't practicable) an attachment order barring dealings without the officer's prior permission.
A copy of any attachment order must be served on the person concerned.
Mandatory 30-day judicial confirmation: the order has 'no effect' unless the Court confirms it within thirty days of being made.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 30-day confirmation deadline is an absolute lapse trigger, not merely directory — an unconfirmed order is treated as having no legal effect at all.
breakdown.how_to_read: The 30-day confirmation clause is the key safeguard to flag for a client whose property has been seized/attached under this section — check the file for whether judicial confirmation actually happened within the window; if not, the order is a nullity.

sections.title: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter
sections.raw_text:
118. Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter.—(1) The Court may appoint the District Magistrate of the area where the property is situated, or any other officer that may be nominated by the District Magistrate, to perform the functions of an Administrator of such property.
    (2) The Administrator appointed under sub-section (1) shall receive and manage the property in relation to which the order has been made under sub-section (1) of section 117 or under section 120 in such manner and subject to such conditions as may be specified by the Central Government.
    (3) The Administrator shall also take such measures, as the Central Government may direct, to dispose of the property which is forfeited to the Central Government.

breakdown.plain_summary: Seized or forfeited property doesn't just sit untouched — someone has to look after it. The Court appoints an "Administrator" (the District Magistrate of the area, or an officer the District Magistrate nominates) to take custody and manage property under a Section 117 seizure/attachment order or a Section 120 forfeiture order, following conditions the Central Government specifies. Once property is finally forfeited to the Central Government, the Administrator is also the one who disposes of it, again per Central Government direction.
essential_elements: Administrator = the District Magistrate of the property's location, or an officer nominated by that District Magistrate.
Manages property under Section 117 (seizure/attachment) or Section 120 (forfeiture) orders.
Management terms and conditions are set by the Central Government.
Disposal of finally-forfeited property is also carried out by the Administrator, per Central Government direction.
breakdown.how_to_read: A short administrative/custodial section — mainly relevant for practitioners handling the practicalities of who physically controls attached or forfeited assets pending the outcome of the Section 119-121 proceedings.

sections.title: Notice of forfeiture of property
sections.raw_text:
119. Notice of forfeiture of property.—(1) If as a result of the inquiry, investigation or survey under section 116, the Court has reason to believe that all or any of such properties are proceeds of crime, it may serve a notice upon such person (hereinafter referred to as the person affected) calling upon him within a period of thirty days specified in the notice to indicate the source of income, earnings or assets, out of which or by means of which he has acquired such property, the evidence on which he relies and other relevant information and particulars, and to show cause why all or any of such properties, as the case may be, should not be declared to be proceeds of crime and forfeited to the Central Government.
    (2) Where a notice under sub-section (1) to any person specifies any property as being held on behalf of such person by any other person, a copy of the notice shall also be served upon such other person.

breakdown.plain_summary: Before any property can actually be forfeited, the person who owns it (the "person affected") must get formal notice and a chance to explain. If the Court, based on the Section 116 investigation, believes property is proceeds of crime, it serves a show-cause notice giving the person thirty days to demonstrate the legitimate source of the property — income, earnings, assets — and the evidence backing that claim, and to argue why the property shouldn't be declared proceeds of crime and forfeited. If the property is nominally held by someone else on the affected person's behalf (a benami-style arrangement), that other person must be served too.
essential_elements: Trigger: reason to believe, from the Section 116 inquiry/investigation/survey, that the property is proceeds of crime.
Notice period: thirty days for the person affected to respond.
Required response content: source of income/earnings/assets, supporting evidence, and other relevant particulars — i.e., why the property shouldn't be forfeited.
Where property is held by a third party on the affected person's behalf, that third party must also be served a copy.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is procedural due process built into a civil forfeiture scheme — failure to serve notice (or to serve a benami holder under sub-section (2)) would be a serious procedural defect.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the natural-justice hinge of the whole forfeiture chain — everything from here to Section 120's actual forfeiture order depends on this notice having been properly issued and served.

sections.title: Forfeiture of property in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
120. Forfeiture of property in certain cases.—(1) The Court may, after considering the explanation, if any, to the show-cause notice issued under section 119 and the material available before it and after giving to the person affected (and in a case where the person affected holds any property specified in the notice through any other person, to such other person also) a reasonable opportunity of being heard, by order, record a finding whether all or any of the properties in question are proceeds of crime:
    Provided that if the person affected (and in a case where the person affected holds any property specified in the notice through any other person such other person also) does not appear before the Court or represent his case before it within a period of thirty days specified in the show-cause notice, the Court may proceed to record a finding under this sub-section ex parte on the basis of evidence available before it.
    (2) Where the Court is satisfied that some of the properties referred to in the show-cause notice are proceeds of crime but it is not possible to identify specifically such properties, then, it shall be lawful for the Court to specify the properties which, to the best of its judgment, are proceeds of crime and record a finding accordingly under sub-section (1).
    (3) Where the Court records a finding under this section to the effect that any property is proceeds of crime, such property shall stand forfeited to the Central Government free from all encumbrances.
    (4) Where any shares in a company stand forfeited to the Central Government under this section, then, the company shall, notwithstanding anything contained in the Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013) or the Articles of Association of the company, forthwith register the Central Government as the transferee of such shares.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the operative forfeiture order itself. After weighing the Section 119 notice explanation (if any) and the material on record, and giving the affected person (and any third-party holder) a real hearing, the Court records a finding on whether the property is proceeds of crime. If the person doesn't show up or make their case within the thirty-day notice window, the Court can still decide the question ex parte on the available evidence — silence or non-appearance doesn't stop the process. Where the Court is satisfied some (but not precisely identifiable) part of the property is tainted, it can use its best judgment to specify which properties count. A positive finding means automatic forfeiture to the Central Government, free of all encumbrances (i.e., wiping out mortgages, liens, and other third-party claims against it) — and if the forfeited property is company shares, the company must immediately re-register the Central Government as the new shareholder, overriding the Companies Act, 2013 or its own Articles of Association if they'd otherwise stand in the way.
essential_elements: Court must consider the Section 119 explanation and material on record, and give a reasonable hearing to the affected person (and any third-party holder).
Ex parte power: non-appearance within the thirty-day notice period lets the Court decide on available evidence alone.
Best-judgment specification power where some (unidentifiable) part of the property is tainted.
Forfeiture effect: automatic vesting in the Central Government, free from all encumbrances.
Share-forfeiture override: the company must register the Central Government as transferee 'notwithstanding' the Companies Act, 2013 or its Articles of Association.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Forfeiture 'free from all encumbrances' extinguishes existing third-party security interests — a serious consequence for anyone who lent against or holds a charge on the property.
The ex parte proviso is a real risk for an affected person who ignores the Section 119 notice — the case can be decided without them.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as directly downstream of Section 119: the notice creates the opportunity to be heard; this section is where that opportunity either bears fruit or, on default, gets bypassed via the ex parte route. Section 121 offers a partial escape hatch (fine in lieu) for mixed-source property.

sections.title: Fine in lieu of forfeiture
sections.raw_text:
121. Fine in lieu of forfeiture.—(1) Where the Court makes a declaration that any property stands forfeited to the Central Government under section 120 and it is a case where the source of only a part of such property has not been proved to the satisfaction of the Court, it shall make an order giving an option to the person affected to pay, in lieu of forfeiture, a fine equal to the market value of such part.
    (2) Before making an order imposing a fine under sub-section (1), the person affected shall be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
    (3) Where the person affected pays the fine due under sub-section (1), within such time as may be allowed in that behalf, the Court may, by order, revoke the declaration of forfeiture under section 120 and thereupon such property shall stand released.

breakdown.plain_summary: A proportionality valve for partial-taint cases. If only part of the property's source is unproven (i.e., some of it is legitimate and only a portion is suspect), the Court doesn't have to forfeit the whole thing — it can instead give the person affected the option to pay a fine equal to the market value of just the tainted part, after a further hearing. Pay the fine on time, and the Court can revoke the Section 120 forfeiture declaration entirely, releasing the property back to the person.
essential_elements: Applies only where the unproven portion is part, not all, of the property.
Fine amount = market value of the unproven part.
A further reasonable opportunity of hearing is required before the fine order is made.
Timely payment lets the Court revoke the forfeiture declaration and release the property.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is an option for the person affected, not a right the Court must grant automatically — read 'shall make an order giving an option' carefully: the option must be offered, but the person must still choose and pay.
Missing the payment deadline forfeits the chance — the property presumably remains forfeited if the fine isn't paid in time.
breakdown.how_to_read: A practical settlement mechanism worth flagging to any client facing a mixed-source forfeiture finding — it can convert a total property loss into a fine calculated on only the tainted fraction.

sections.title: Certain transfers to be null and void
sections.raw_text: 122. Certain transfers to be null and void.—Where after the making of an order under sub-section (1) of section 117 or the issue of a notice under section 119, any property referred to in the said order or notice is transferred by any mode whatsoever such transfers shall, for the purposes of the proceedings under this Chapter, be ignored and if such property is subsequently forfeited to the Central Government under section 120, then, the transfer of such property shall be deemed to be null and void.

breakdown.plain_summary: An anti-evasion backstop closing the obvious loophole: once a Section 117 seizure/attachment order or a Section 119 forfeiture notice has been issued, any transfer of the affected property — sale, gift, any mode at all — is simply ignored for the purposes of the Chapter VIII proceedings. If the property is ultimately forfeited under Section 120, that intervening transfer is deemed null and void, meaning the person can't defeat forfeiture by quickly signing the property away to a relative or associate.
essential_elements: Trigger point: any transfer occurring after a Section 117 order or a Section 119 notice.
Such a transfer is disregarded for the purposes of the Chapter VIII proceedings, regardless of its mode.
If forfeiture under Section 120 later follows, the transfer is deemed null and void retrospectively.
breakdown.how_to_read: A short but powerful section — flag it whenever a client's forfeiture-exposed property shows a suspiciously timed post-notice transfer; that transfer offers no protection.

sections.title: Procedure in respect of letter of request
sections.raw_text: 123. Procedure in respect of letter of request.—Every letter of request, summons or warrant, received by the Central Government from, and every letter of request, summons or warrant, to be transmitted to a contracting State under this Chapter shall be transmitted to a contracting State or, as the case may be, sent to the concerned Court in India in such form and in such manner as the Central Government may, by notification, specify in this behalf.

breakdown.plain_summary: A catch-all procedural section confirming that every inbound or outbound letter of request, summons, or warrant handled under Chapter VIII travels in whatever form and by whatever manner the Central Government notifies — a single, government-controlled transmission protocol for all of the Chapter's cross-border traffic.
essential_elements: Covers both directions: received-from and to-be-transmitted-to a contracting State.
Form and manner of transmission are fixed by Central Government notification.
breakdown.how_to_read: Purely procedural glue tying together Sections 110-122's various letter-of-request mechanisms into one uniform transmission channel.

sections.title: Application of this Chapter
sections.raw_text: 124. Application of this Chapter.—The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that the application of this Chapter in relation to a contracting State with which reciprocal arrangements have been made, shall be subject to such conditions, exceptions or qualifications as are specified in the said notification.

breakdown.plain_summary: The closing section of Chapter VIII gives the Central Government flexibility to fine-tune how the whole reciprocal-assistance chapter applies to any particular contracting State — by Gazette notification it can impose conditions, carve out exceptions, or add qualifications specific to that country's arrangement, rather than applying the Chapter uniformly and rigidly to every contracting State alike.
essential_elements: Mechanism: notification in the Official Gazette.
Applies chapter-wide, but can be tailored per contracting State.
Can impose conditions, exceptions, or qualifications on the Chapter's application.
breakdown.how_to_read: A standard closing 'Central Government may modify by notification' clause — practically relevant for checking whether a specific country's reciprocal arrangement carries any special conditions before relying on the general Chapter VIII procedure.

sections.title: Security for keeping peace on conviction

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter IX and is the post-conviction route into "peace security." When a Court of Session or a first-class Magistrate convicts someone of certain public-order-related offences — offences against the public tranquillity chapter of the BNS, assault/criminal force/mischief offences, criminal intimidation, or any offence that caused or threatened a breach of the peace — the Court can, as part of sentencing, additionally order the person to execute a bond to keep the peace for up to three years. This is preventive, not punitive: it's a forward-looking guarantee layered on top of the sentence itself. If the underlying conviction later gets overturned on appeal or otherwise, the bond automatically becomes void — it has no independent life apart from the conviction that triggered it. Appellate and Revisional Courts can also make this order, not just the trial Court.
essential_elements: Triggering Courts: Court of Session, or a Magistrate of the first class.
Triggering event: conviction for a listed offence (or abetment of one) under sub-section (2).
The order is made 'at the time of passing sentence' — it rides alongside the sentence, not separately.
Maximum bond period: three years, at the Court's discretion within that ceiling.
Automatic voidance if the conviction is set aside on appeal or otherwise.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Certain BNS Chapter XI offences are expressly excluded from triggering this section — sub-sections (1) of section 193, section 196, and section 197 of the BNS.
Appellate and Revisional Courts share this power with the original convicting Court — it's not confined to the trial forum.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sub-section (2) as a checklist — this section only applies if the conviction falls into one of the four listed categories. The three-year ceiling and the automatic-voidance-on-reversal rule (sub-section 3) are the two numbers/triggers worth remembering for practice.

sections.title: Security for keeping peace in other cases
sections.raw_text:
126. Security for keeping peace in other cases.—(1) When an Executive Magistrate receives information that any person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquillity or to do any wrongful act that may probably occasion a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquillity and is of opinion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding, he may, in the manner hereinafter provided, require such person to show cause why he should not be ordered to execute a bond or bail bond for keeping the peace for such period, not exceeding one year, as the Magistrate thinks fit.
    (2) Proceedings under this section may be taken before any Executive Magistrate when either the place where the breach of the peace or disturbance is apprehended is within his local jurisdiction or there is within such jurisdiction a person who is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquillity or to do any wrongful act as aforesaid beyond such jurisdiction.

breakdown.plain_summary: The preventive (pre-conviction) counterpart to Section 125. No conviction is needed here at all — an Executive Magistrate who receives credible information that a person is likely to breach the peace, disturb public tranquillity, or do some wrongful act likely to cause either of those, can start proceedings requiring the person to show cause why they shouldn't be bound over to keep the peace, for up to one year. Jurisdiction is flexible: proceedings can be brought either where the anticipated trouble will occur, or where the person likely to cause it is currently located, even if the trouble itself is expected to happen elsewhere.
essential_elements: No conviction required — purely preventive, based on 'information' received by the Executive Magistrate.
Threshold: the Magistrate must form an opinion that there is 'sufficient ground for proceeding.'
Maximum bond period: one year (shorter than Section 125's three-year ceiling, reflecting its lower evidentiary threshold).
Dual jurisdictional basis: either the place of anticipated breach, or the place where the suspected person is located.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a show-cause proceeding, not a summary order — the person gets a chance to respond before any bond is actually imposed (the full inquiry procedure is in Sections 130-137).
breakdown.how_to_read: Contrast directly with Section 125: this is the 'no conviction yet' preventive track, with a lower one-year ceiling. Sections 130 onward supply the common procedural machinery shared by Sections 126-129.

sections.title: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters
sections.raw_text:
127. Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters.—(1) When an Executive Magistrate receives information that there is within his local jurisdiction any person who, within or without such jurisdiction,—
        (i) either orally or in writing or in any other manner, intentionally disseminates or attempts to disseminate or abets the dissemination of,—
            (a) any matter the publication of which is punishable under section 152 or section 196 or section 197 or section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (45 of 2023); or
            (b) any matter concerning a Judge acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duties which amounts to criminal intimidation or defamation under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023;
        (ii) makes, produces, publishes or keeps for sale, imports, exports, conveys, sells, lets to hire, distributes, publicly exhibits or in any other manner puts into circulation any obscene matter such as is referred to in section 294 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023,
and the Magistrate is of opinion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding, the Magistrate may, in the manner hereinafter provided, require such person to show cause why he should not be ordered to execute a bond or bail bond, for his good behaviour for such period, not exceeding one year, as the Magistrate thinks fit.
    (2) No proceedings shall be taken under this section against the editor, proprietor, printer or publisher of any publication registered under, and edited, printed and published in conformity with, the rules laid down in the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867 (25 of 1867) with reference to any matter contained in such publication except by the order or under the authority of the State Government or some officer empowered by the State Government in this behalf.
key_terms: press and registration of books act

breakdown.plain_summary: A targeted "good behaviour" security provision aimed at people who spread dangerous or unlawful content — matter punishable under specific BNS provisions (covering things like sedition-adjacent offences, promoting enmity, statements prejudicial to national integration, or imperilling public order), criminally intimidating or defaming material against a Judge acting in official capacity, or obscene material under BNS Section 294 (covering its production, sale, import/export, distribution, or public exhibition). If an Executive Magistrate has sufficient ground, they can require the person to show cause why they shouldn't execute a good-behaviour bond for up to one year. A special press-freedom safeguard applies: registered-publication editors/proprietors/printers/publishers acting within the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867 framework can't be proceeded against under this section except with State Government authorisation — an extra procedural gate protecting the press specifically.
essential_elements: Covers two categories: (i) intentional dissemination (or abetment) of specified unlawful/prejudicial matter, including anti-Judge criminal intimidation/defamation; (ii) production/circulation of obscene matter under BNS Section 294.
Dissemination can occur 'within or without' the Magistrate's jurisdiction — the person just needs to be located within it.
Maximum bond period: one year, same ceiling as Section 126.
Press safeguard: registered publications' editors/proprietors/printers/publishers are shielded unless the State Government (or its delegate) authorises proceedings.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The press-safeguard proviso in sub-section (2) is a specific carve-out, not a blanket immunity for all publishers — only registered, properly-conducted publications under the 1867 Act qualify, and even then State Government authorisation can override the shield.
breakdown.how_to_read: Notice the press-freedom proviso is doing real constitutional work here (balancing Article 19(1)(a) against public order) — flag it whenever a media client is targeted under this section.

sections.title: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons
sections.raw_text: 128. Security for good behaviour from suspected persons.—When an Executive Magistrate receives information that there is within his local jurisdiction a person taking precautions to conceal his presence and that there is reason to believe that he is doing so with a view to committing a cognizable offence, the Magistrate may, in the manner hereinafter provided, require such person to show cause why he should not be ordered to execute a bond or bail bond for his good behaviour for such period, not exceeding one year, as the Magistrate thinks fit.

breakdown.plain_summary: A narrow, suspicion-based preventive-detention-adjacent provision: if a person is deliberately hiding their presence within the Magistrate's jurisdiction, and there's reason to believe they're doing so in preparation for a cognizable offence, the Magistrate can require a good-behaviour bond, for up to one year, via the standard show-cause procedure.
essential_elements: Two-part threshold: (a) the person is taking active precautions to conceal their presence, and (b) reason to believe this concealment is aimed at committing a cognizable offence.
Maximum bond period: one year.
Follows the common procedure laid down in Sections 130 onward.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Mere concealment alone is not enough — it must be coupled with 'reason to believe' a cognizable offence is being planned; innocent reasons for concealment (e.g., avoiding harassment, personal safety) don't satisfy the threshold.
breakdown.how_to_read: Short and self-contained — the whole test is in the single sentence. Compare its narrower scope against Section 129's much longer list of specific habitual-offender categories.

sections.title: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

breakdown.plain_summary: The longest and broadest of the good-behaviour categories, aimed squarely at habitual criminals. It lists seven overlapping categories: habitual robbers/house-breakers/thieves/forgers; habitual knowing receivers of stolen property; habitual protectors/harbourers of thieves or handlers of stolen property; habitual kidnapping/abduction/extortion/cheating/mischief offenders (or offences under the BNS's public-tranquillity-adjacent Chapter X or specific public-servant-related sections); habitual breach-of-the-peace offenders; habitual offenders under a named list of regulatory statutes (Drugs and Cosmetics, Foreigners Act, EPF Act, Essential Commodities, Protection of Civil Rights, Customs, Food Safety) or any other hoarding/profiteering/adulteration/corruption law; and finally a catch-all — anyone "so desperate and dangerous" that being at large without security would be hazardous to the community. Uniquely among this quartet of good-behaviour sections, this one carries the longer three-year maximum bond period (matching Section 125's post-conviction ceiling), reflecting the seriousness of chronic, repeat offending it targets.
essential_elements: Seven distinct qualifying categories (a)-(g), any one of which suffices.
'Habitually' is the recurring qualifier for most categories — a single incident generally won't do; a pattern is required.
Category (f) incorporates a specific list of regulatory/economic-offence statutes plus a residual clause for hoarding/profiteering/adulteration/corruption laws generally.
Category (g) is a broad residual 'desperate and dangerous' catch-all independent of any specific offence pattern.
Maximum bond period: three years — the longest among the preventive (non-conviction) good-behaviour sections.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'habit' element under sections 128, 129 categories (a)-(f) can be proved by evidence of general repute, not just specific proven instances — see Section 135(4) later in this Chapter, which supplies the evidentiary rule.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat categories (a)-(f) as fact-specific pigeonholes to check the person against, and category (g) as the fallback if none of the specific categories quite fit but the person is still clearly dangerous. Remember the cross-reference to Section 135(4) for how 'habit' gets proved at the inquiry stage.

sections.title: Order to be made
sections.raw_text: 130. Order to be made.—When a Magistrate acting under section 126, section 127, section 128 or section 129, deems it necessary to require any person to show cause under such section, he shall make an order in writing, setting forth the substance of the information received, the amount of the bond to be executed, the term for which it is to be in force and the number of sureties, after considering the sufficiency and fitness of sureties.

breakdown.plain_summary: The formal gateway order that kicks off the show-cause procedure under any of Sections 126-129. It must be in writing and specify four things: the substance of the information received, the bond amount, how long the bond will run, and the number of sureties required — the Magistrate must have already turned their mind to the sufficiency and fitness of sureties before issuing it.
essential_elements: Applies uniformly across all four preventive-security grounds: Sections 126, 127, 128, and 129.
Mandatory written order — not oral.
Must state: substance of information, bond amount, bond duration, and number of sureties.
The Magistrate must have already considered surety sufficiency and fitness before making the order.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the procedural hinge connecting the four substantive grounds (Sections 126-129) to the common inquiry machinery that follows (Sections 131 onward) — every peace/good-behaviour case, regardless of which ground triggered it, starts here.

sections.title: Procedure in respect of person present in Court
sections.raw_text: 131. Procedure in respect of person present in Court.—If the person in respect of whom such order is made is present in Court, it shall be read over to him, or, if he so desires, the substance thereof shall be explained to him.

breakdown.plain_summary: A simple fair-notice rule: if the person against whom a Section 130 order is made happens to already be present in Court, the order must be read out to them (or, if they'd prefer, its substance explained), so they understand exactly what they're being asked to show cause about.
essential_elements: Applies only where the person is already present in Court when the order is made.
Two options: the order is read out verbatim, or its substance is explained if the person prefers.
breakdown.how_to_read: Short procedural section — its counterpart for a person not present in Court is Section 132, immediately following.

sections.title: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present
sections.raw_text:
132. Summons or warrant in case of person not so present.—If such person is not present in Court, the Magistrate shall issue a summons requiring him to appear, or, when such person is in custody, a warrant directing the officer in whose custody he is to bring him before the Court:
    Provided that whenever it appears to such Magistrate, upon the report of a police officer or upon other information (the substance of which report or information shall be recorded by the Magistrate), that there is reason to fear the commission of a breach of the peace, and that such breach of the peace cannot be prevented otherwise than by the immediate arrest of such person, the Magistrate may at any time issue a warrant for his arrest.

breakdown.plain_summary: The mirror image of Section 131 for a person who isn't already in Court: the Magistrate issues a summons to bring them in, or, if they're already in custody for some other reason, a warrant directing the custodial officer to produce them. There's an emergency override: if the Magistrate has reason to fear an imminent breach of the peace that can only be averted by immediate arrest, they can skip straight to an arrest warrant at any time — bypassing the ordinary summons-first approach.
essential_elements: Default route: summons to appear (person not in custody) or warrant to the custodial officer (person already in custody).
Emergency override: immediate arrest warrant where breach of the peace is feared and cannot otherwise be prevented.
The report or information grounding the emergency override must be recorded in substance by the Magistrate.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The emergency-arrest proviso is available 'at any time' — it isn't limited to the initial stage, and can override the ordinary summons-first sequence whenever the urgency threshold is met.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair with Section 133 immediately following — every summons or warrant issued under this section must carry a copy of the Section 130 order.

sections.title: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant
sections.raw_text: 133. Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant.—Every summons or warrant issued under section 132 shall be accompanied by a copy of the order made under section 130, and such copy shall be delivered by the officer serving or executing such summons or warrant to the person served with, or arrested under, the same.

breakdown.plain_summary: A fair-notice safeguard mirroring Section 131 for people who weren't already in Court: whenever a Section 132 summons or warrant is issued, a copy of the underlying Section 130 order must travel with it and actually be delivered to the person when served or arrested — so an arrested or summoned person always knows the specific grounds (information, bond terms, sureties required) behind the process against them.
essential_elements: Applies to every summons or warrant issued under Section 132.
The copy of the Section 130 order must be physically delivered to the person served or arrested.
breakdown.how_to_read: Closes the loop opened by Sections 131-132 — between the two, every person subject to a Section 130 order gets to know its contents, whether present in Court or brought in later.

sections.title: Power to dispense with personal attendance
sections.raw_text: 134. Power to dispense with personal attendance.—The Magistrate may, if he sees sufficient cause, dispense with the personal attendance of any person called upon to show cause why he should not be ordered to execute a bond for keeping the peace or for good behaviour and may permit him to appear by an advocate.

breakdown.plain_summary: A convenience/dignity provision: the person called upon to show cause doesn't necessarily have to attend in person throughout — if the Magistrate sees sufficient cause, they can dispense with personal attendance and let the person be represented by an advocate instead.
essential_elements: Discretionary power — the Magistrate must see 'sufficient cause' before dispensing with personal attendance.
The alternative is representation by an advocate.
breakdown.how_to_read: A practical relief provision — useful to invoke for a client who faces genuine hardship attending every hearing of a good-behaviour/peace-security inquiry.

sections.title: Inquiry as to truth of information
sections.raw_text:
135. Inquiry as to truth of information.—(1) When an order under section 130 has been read or explained under section 131 to a person present in Court, or when any person appears or is brought before a Magistrate in compliance with, or in execution of, a summons or warrant, issued under section 132, the Magistrate shall proceed to inquire into the truth of the information upon which action has been taken, and to take such further evidence as may appear necessary.
    (2) Such inquiry shall be made, as nearly as may be practicable, in the manner hereinafter prescribed for conducting trial and recording evidence in summons-cases.
    (3) After the commencement, and before the completion, of the inquiry under sub-section (1), the Magistrate, if he considers that immediate measures are necessary for the prevention of a breach of the peace or disturbance of the public tranquillity or the commission of any offence or for the public safety, may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, direct the person in respect of whom the order under section 130 has been made to execute a bond or bail bond, for keeping the peace or maintaining good behaviour until the conclusion of the inquiry, and may detain him in custody until such bond or bail bond is executed or, in default of execution, until the inquiry is concluded:
    Provided that—
        (a) no person against whom proceedings are not being taken under section 127, section 128, or section 129 shall be directed to execute a bond or bail bond for maintaining good behaviour;
        (b) the conditions of such bond, whether as to the amount thereof or as to the provision of sureties or the number thereof or the pecuniary extent of their liability, shall not be more onerous than those specified in the order under section 130.
    (4) For the purposes of this section the fact that a person is a habitual offender or is so desperate and dangerous as to render his being at large without security hazardous to the community may be proved by evidence of general repute or otherwise.
    (5) Where two or more persons have been associated together in the matter under inquiry, they may be dealt with in the same or separate inquiries as the Magistrate shall think just.
    (6) The inquiry under this section shall be completed within a period of six months from the date of its commencement, and if such inquiry is not so completed, the proceedings under this Chapter shall, on the expiry of the said period, stand terminated unless, for special reasons to be recorded in writing, the Magistrate otherwise directs:
    Provided that where any person has been kept in detention pending such inquiry, the proceeding against that person, unless terminated earlier, shall stand terminated on the expiry of a period of six months of such detention.
    (7) Where any direction is made under sub-section (6) permitting the continuance of proceedings, the Sessions Judge may, on an application made to him by the aggrieved party, vacate such direction if he is satisfied that it was not based on any special reason or was perverse.

breakdown.plain_summary: The heart of the Chapter IX procedure — the actual inquiry into whether the Section 130 order's underlying information is true. It runs roughly like a summons-case trial (evidence recording, etc.). Mid-inquiry, if the Magistrate thinks immediate action is needed to prevent a breach of the peace, disturbance, an offence, or for public safety, they can order an interim bond (and detain the person if they don't comply) pending the inquiry's conclusion — but only for people actually facing good-behaviour proceedings under Sections 127-129 (not the plain peace-keeping track), and the interim bond terms can't be harsher than what the original Section 130 order specified. For habitual-offender or "desperate and dangerous" findings, general repute evidence is expressly allowed, not just specific proven acts. Multiple associated persons can be inquired into jointly or separately, at the Magistrate's discretion.
