There's a hard six-month completion deadline — miss it, and proceedings automatically terminate (with an even harder rule if the person has been detained: termination at six months of detention regardless), unless the Magistrate records special reasons to continue, and even that continuation is subject to Sessions Judge review on an aggrieved party's application if the special reasons look pretextual or perverse.
essential_elements: Inquiry follows the summons-case trial procedure, as nearly as practicable.
Interim bond power during the inquiry: available only for good-behaviour proceedings (Sections 127-129), on recorded reasons, capped at the original order's terms.
General-repute evidence is expressly permissible to prove habitual-offender or desperate-and-dangerous status.
Six-month hard deadline for completing the inquiry, with automatic termination on expiry absent recorded special reasons.
A stricter six-month cap applies specifically where the person has been detained pending inquiry.
Sessions Judge oversight: can vacate a continuation direction found not to rest on genuine special reasons, or found perverse.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The interim-bond power under sub-section (3) is expressly unavailable for pure peace-keeping proceedings (Section 126) — only good-behaviour tracks (127-129) permit it.
The six-month detention cap is an independent, stricter ceiling that overrides the general six-month inquiry deadline where actual detention has occurred.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the longest and most procedurally dense section in the Chapter — read the six-month deadline and its detention-specific proviso as the key liberty safeguard, and the Sessions Judge review in sub-section (7) as the check against Magistrates rubber-stamping indefinite extensions.

sections.title: Order to give security

breakdown.plain_summary: The final, operative order following a completed Section 135 inquiry — if the inquiry proves the security is actually necessary, the Magistrate must order it. Three built-in limits protect the person: the final bond can't exceed the nature, amount, or duration set out in the original Section 130 order (no escalation after the fact); the amount must be reasonable and not excessive given the case's circumstances; and — a specific child-protection rule — if the person is a child, they personally cannot be made to execute the bond at all; only sureties on the child's behalf can.
essential_elements: Triggered only if the inquiry proves necessity for keeping the peace or maintaining good behaviour.
Cap: the final security cannot exceed the nature, amount, or period specified in the Section 130 order.
The bond amount must be fixed with due regard to the case's circumstances and must not be excessive.
Child-specific rule: a bond in respect of a child must be executed only by sureties, never by the child personally.
breakdown.how_to_read: The child proviso (c) is the standout safeguard here — always check the age of the person concerned before an order under this section is finalised.

sections.title: Discharge of person informed against
sections.raw_text: 137. Discharge of person informed against.—If, on an inquiry under section 135, it is not proved that it is necessary for keeping the peace or maintaining good behaviour, as the case may be, that the person in respect of whom the inquiry is made, should execute a bond, the Magistrate shall make an entry on the record to that effect, and if such person is in custody only for the purposes of the inquiry, shall release him, or, if such person is not in custody, shall discharge him.

breakdown.plain_summary: The flip side of Section 136 — if the inquiry fails to prove that security is necessary, the person must be let go. The Magistrate records this outcome formally, and if the person was held in custody solely for the inquiry, they're released; if never in custody, they're simply discharged from the proceedings.
essential_elements: Triggered when the inquiry fails to prove necessity.
A formal record entry of this outcome is mandatory.
In-custody-for-the-inquiry-only persons are released; not-in-custody persons are discharged.
breakdown.how_to_read: The natural counterpart to Section 136 — every Section 135 inquiry ends in one or the other of these two outcomes.

sections.title: Commencement of period for which security is required
sections.raw_text:
138. Commencement of period for which security is required.—(1) If any person, in respect of whom an order requiring security is made under section 125 or section 136, is at the time such order is made, sentenced to, or undergoing a sentence of, imprisonment, the period for which such security is required shall commence on the expiration of such sentence.
    (2) In other cases such period shall commence on the date of such order unless the Magistrate, for sufficient reason, fixes a later date.

breakdown.plain_summary: Clarifies when the clock actually starts running on a security order made under either Section 125 (post-conviction) or Section 136 (post-inquiry). If the person is already serving (or has just been sentenced to) imprisonment when the order is made, the security period only begins once that sentence ends — it doesn't run concurrently with imprisonment, since the person poses no liberty-related risk while locked up. In all other cases, the period starts from the date of the order itself, unless the Magistrate has sufficient reason to fix a later start date.
essential_elements: Applies to security orders under Section 125 or Section 136.
If the person is under (or sentenced to) imprisonment: the security period starts only when that sentence expires.
Otherwise: the period starts on the date of the order, unless the Magistrate fixes a later date for sufficient reason.
breakdown.how_to_read: A short but practically important timing rule — always check whether the person concerned was serving a sentence at the time of the order before calculating when a peace/good-behaviour bond period actually begins and ends.

sections.title: Contents of bond
sections.raw_text: 139. Contents of bond.—The bond or bail bond to be executed by any such person shall bind him to keep the peace or to be of good behaviour, as the case may be, and in the latter case the commission or attempt to commit, or the abetment of, any offence punishable with imprisonment, wherever it may be committed, is a breach of the bond or bail bond.

breakdown.plain_summary: Defines what the bond actually promises. A "keep the peace" bond binds the person simply to that. A "good behaviour" bond is broader in its breach trigger: committing, attempting, or abetting any imprisonable offence — anywhere, not just within the Magistrate's jurisdiction — counts as a breach of the bond.
essential_elements: Two bond types with different content: 'keep the peace' vs. 'good behaviour.'
For good-behaviour bonds specifically: any commission, attempt, or abetment of an imprisonable offence is a breach, regardless of where it's committed.
breakdown.how_to_read: Note how much broader the good-behaviour trigger is compared to keep-the-peace — an unrelated offence committed far away can still breach a good-behaviour bond, which is a key point for anyone advising a person currently bound under one.

sections.title: Power to reject sureties
sections.raw_text:
140. Power to reject sureties.—(1) A Magistrate may refuse to accept any surety offered, or may reject any surety previously accepted by him or his predecessor under this Chapter on the ground that such surety is an unfit person for the purposes of the bail bond:
    Provided that before so refusing to accept or rejecting any such surety, he shall either himself hold an inquiry on oath into the fitness of the surety, or cause such inquiry to be held and a report to be made thereon by a Magistrate subordinate to him.
    (2) Such Magistrate shall, before holding the inquiry, give reasonable notice to the surety and to the person by whom the surety was offered and shall, in making the inquiry, record the substance of the evidence adduced before him.
    (3) If the Magistrate is satisfied, after considering the evidence so adduced either before him or before a Magistrate deputed under sub-section (1), and the report of such Magistrate (if any), that the surety is an unfit person for the purposes of the bail bond, he shall make an order refusing to accept or rejecting, as the case may be, such surety and recording his reasons for so doing:
    Provided that before making an order rejecting any surety who has previously been accepted, the Magistrate shall issue his summons or warrant, as he thinks fit, and cause the person for whom the surety is bound to appear or to be brought before him.

breakdown.plain_summary: Gives the Magistrate quality control over sureties — both at the offering stage and even after a surety has already been accepted (by the same Magistrate or a predecessor). Rejection can't be arbitrary: a formal on-oath fitness inquiry (held personally or delegated to a subordinate Magistrate who reports back) is mandatory first, with reasonable notice to both the surety and the person who offered them, and a recorded evidentiary record. Only after that inquiry, and only with recorded reasons, can the Magistrate reject the surety. If a previously-accepted surety is being rejected (as opposed to a fresh offer being refused), there's an extra procedural step: the person for whom the surety stood must be summoned or brought before the Magistrate before the rejection order is made.
essential_elements: Applies to both fresh surety offers and previously-accepted sureties.
Mandatory fitness inquiry on oath before any refusal/rejection — either held personally or delegated with a report back.
Reasonable notice must be given to both the surety and the person who offered the surety.
Rejection requires recorded reasons.
Rejecting a previously-accepted surety additionally requires summoning/producing the person for whom the surety is bound before the order is made.
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the escalating procedural protection: rejecting a brand-new offer needs the fitness inquiry; rejecting an already-accepted surety needs that plus the additional summons/production step — reflecting the greater disruption caused by pulling the rug out from under an existing arrangement.

sections.title: Imprisonment in default of security
sections.raw_text:
141. Imprisonment in default of security.—(1)(a) If any person ordered to give security under section 125 or section 136 does not give such security on or before the date on which the period for which such security is to be given commences, he shall, except in the case next hereinafter mentioned, be committed to prison, or, if he is already in prison, be detained in prison until such period expires or until within such period he gives the security to the Court or Magistrate who made the order requiring it;
    (b) if any person after having executed a bond or bail bond for keeping the peace in pursuance of an order of a Magistrate under section 136, is proved, to the satisfaction of such Magistrate or his successor-in-office, to have committed breach of the bond or bail bond, such Magistrate or successor-in-office may, after recording the grounds of such proof, order that the person be arrested and detained in prison until the expiry of the period of the bond or bail bond and such order shall be without prejudice to any other punishment or forfeiture to which the said person may be liable in accordance with law.
    (2) When such person has been ordered by a Magistrate to give security for a period exceeding one year, such Magistrate shall, if such person does not give such security as aforesaid, issue a warrant directing him to be detained in prison pending the orders of the Sessions Judge and the proceedings shall be laid, as soon as conveniently may be, before such Court.
    (3) Such Court, after examining such proceedings and requiring from the Magistrate any further information or evidence which it thinks necessary, and after giving the concerned person a reasonable opportunity of being heard, may pass such order on the case as it thinks fit:
    Provided that the period (if any) for which any person is imprisoned for failure to give security shall not exceed three years.
    (4) If security has been required in the course of the same proceeding from two or more persons in respect of any one of whom the proceedings are referred to the Sessions Judge under sub-section (2) such reference shall also include the case of any other of such persons who has been ordered to give security, and the provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3) shall, in that event, apply to the case of such other person also, except that the period (if any) for which he may be imprisoned, shall not exceed the period for which he was ordered to give security.
    (5) A Sessions Judge may in his discretion transfer any proceedings laid before him under sub-section (2) or sub-section (4) to an Additional Sessions Judge and upon such transfer, such Additional Sessions Judge may exercise the powers of a Sessions Judge under this section in respect of such proceedings.
    (6) If the security is tendered to the officer in charge of the jail, he shall forthwith refer the matter to the Court or Magistrate who made the order, and shall await the orders of such Court or Magistrate.
    (7) Imprisonment for failure to give security for keeping the peace shall be simple.
    (8) Imprisonment for failure to give security for good behaviour shall, where the proceedings have been taken under section 127, be simple, and, where the proceedings have been taken under section 128 or section 129, be rigorous or simple as the Court or Magistrate in each case directs.

breakdown.plain_summary: The enforcement teeth of the whole Chapter: what happens if a person ordered to give security under Section 125 or 136 simply doesn't. Default consequence: committal to (or continued detention in) prison until the security period expires or the security is actually given. Separately, breach of an already-executed peace-keeping bond can itself lead to arrest and imprisonment for the bond's remaining period, on recorded proof of the breach — and this is on top of, not instead of, any other legal punishment the breach might attract. There's a jurisdictional escalation for longer orders: if the required security period exceeds one year, the Magistrate can't just imprison the person on their own authority — they must refer the matter to the Sessions Judge, who reviews the record, can call for more evidence, must give the person a hearing, and then decides — subject to an absolute three-year cap on imprisonment for security default. Multiple co-accused persons from the same proceeding get bundled into the same Sessions Judge reference if any one of them triggers it, though each person's own imprisonment cap tracks their own originally-ordered security period. A Sessions Judge can delegate to an Additional Sessions Judge. Tendering the security to the jail officer (rather than the Court directly) is expressly allowed — the jail officer just refers it up. Finally, the type of imprisonment differs by track: peace-keeping default is always simple imprisonment; good-behaviour default is simple for Section 127 (dissemination) cases, but the Court/Magistrate's choice between rigorous or simple for Sections 128-129 (suspected persons / habitual offenders) cases.
essential_elements: Default consequence: committal to or continued detention in prison until the security is given or the period expires.
Bond breach (post-execution) can independently trigger arrest and imprisonment for the bond's unexpired period, without prejudice to other legal consequences.
Mandatory Sessions Judge reference where the required security period exceeds one year — the Magistrate cannot imprison unilaterally in such cases.
Absolute cap: imprisonment for security default cannot exceed three years.
Imprisonment type varies by track: simple for peace-keeping and Section 127 good-behaviour defaults; Court/Magistrate's choice of simple or rigorous for Section 128/129 defaults.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Multiple-persons bundling under sub-section (4) still respects each individual's own security-period cap when fixing their imprisonment term.
Tendering security directly to the jail officer under sub-section (6) is a valid alternative channel — the officer must refer it onward and await orders, not decide unilaterally.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the section to reach for whenever advising a detained client on a peace/good-behaviour bond default — check first whether the required period exceeded one year (Sessions Judge reference required), then check the three-year absolute ceiling, then check which imprisonment type applies to their specific track.

sections.title: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security
sections.raw_text:
142. Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security.—(1) Whenever the District Magistrate in the case of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under section 136, or the Chief Judicial Magistrate in any other case is of opinion that any person imprisoned for failing to give security under this Chapter may be released without hazard to the community or to any other person, he may order such person to be discharged.
    (2) Whenever any person has been imprisoned for failing to give security under this Chapter, the High Court or Court of Session, or, where the order was made by any other Court, District Magistrate, in the case of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under section 136, or the Chief Judicial Magistrate in any other case, may make an order reducing the amount of the security or the number of sureties or the time for which security has been required.
    (3) An order under sub-section (1) may direct the discharge of such person either without conditions or upon any conditions which such person accepts:
    Provided that any condition imposed shall cease to be operative when the period for which such person was ordered to give security has expired.
    (4) The State Government may prescribe, by rules, the conditions upon which a conditional discharge may be made.
    (5) If any condition upon which any person has been discharged is, in the opinion of District Magistrate, in the case of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under section 136, or the Chief Judicial Magistrate in any other case by whom the order of discharge was made or of his successor, not fulfilled, he may cancel the same.
    (6) When a conditional order of discharge has been cancelled under sub-section (5), such person may be arrested by any police officer without warrant, and shall thereupon be produced before the District Magistrate, in the case of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under section 136, or the Chief Judicial Magistrate in any other case.
    (7) Unless such person gives security in accordance with the terms of the original order for the unexpired portion of the term for which he was in the first instance committed or ordered to be detained (such portion being deemed to be a period equal to the period between the date of the breach of the conditions of discharge and the date on which, except for such conditional discharge, he would have been entitled to release), District Magistrate, in the case of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under section 136, or the Chief Judicial Magistrate in any other case may remand such person to prison to undergo such unexpired portion.
    (8) A person remanded to prison under sub-section (7) shall, subject to the provisions of section 141, be released at any time on giving security in accordance with the terms of the original order for the unexpired portion aforesaid to the Court or Magistrate by whom such order was made, or to its or his successor.
    (9) The High Court or Court of Session may at any time, for sufficient reasons to be recorded in writing, cancel any bond for keeping the peace or for good behaviour executed under this Chapter by any order made by it, and District Magistrate, in the case of an order passed by an Executive Magistrate under section 136, or the Chief Judicial Magistrate in any other case may make such cancellation where such bond was executed under his order or under the order of any other Court in his district.
    (10) Any surety for the peaceable conduct or good behaviour of another person ordered to execute a bond under this Chapter may at any time apply to the Court making such order to cancel the bond and on such application being made, the Court shall issue a summons or warrant, as it thinks fit, requiring the person for whom such surety is bound to appear or to be brought before it.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Chapter's safety-valve/clemency section, closing it out. It gives senior authorities — the District Magistrate (for Executive Magistrate orders under Section 136) or the Chief Judicial Magistrate (for other cases) — power to release, on their own opinion, a person imprisoned for security default who can safely be let out without hazarding the community. Separately, the High Court, Court of Session, or the same District Magistrate/Chief Judicial Magistrate can reduce the security amount, number of sureties, or the time period, easing the terms without a full release. Release can be unconditional or conditional (conditions automatically lapse once the original security period would have expired anyway); the State Government can prescribe by rule what kinds of conditions are permissible. If a conditionally-discharged person breaches their conditions, they can be re-arrested without warrant and brought before the releasing authority, then remanded to serve out the unexpired portion of their original sentence unless they now give the required security — though they can still buy their way out at any point during that remand by finally giving the security. Independently, the High Court/Court of Session (or the District Magistrate/Chief Judicial Magistrate in their own district) can cancel any peace/good-behaviour bond outright for recorded sufficient reasons. And finally, a surety themselves — not just the principal — can apply to be released from their own surety obligation, triggering a summons/warrant to bring the principal back before the Court to sort out a replacement arrangement.
essential_elements: Release power vested in the District Magistrate (Section 136 orders) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (other cases), on their opinion that release is safe.
Separate power (High Court/Sessions Court or District/Chief Judicial Magistrate) to reduce security amount, surety count, or time period without full release.
Conditional discharge is permitted; conditions automatically lapse at the original security period's expiry; the State Government can prescribe permissible conditions by rule.
Breach of discharge conditions: warrantless arrest, production before the releasing authority, and possible remand for the unexpired portion — avoidable by finally furnishing the security.
Independent bond-cancellation power for the High Court/Sessions Court (any time, recorded reasons) or the District/Chief Judicial Magistrate (within their own district's orders).
A surety can apply to be discharged from their own obligation, triggering process to bring the principal back before the Court.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'unexpired portion' calculation on remand under sub-section (7) is specifically tied to the gap between the conditional-discharge breach date and the date the person would otherwise have been entitled to release — not simply the full original term.
Remand under sub-section (7) remains subject to Section 141's rules (e.g., the three-year absolute imprisonment cap), so it isn't an unlimited re-imprisonment power.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this as the release/relief counterpart to Section 141's enforcement machinery — whenever a client has been imprisoned for security default, this is the section to check for a path back out, whether via outright release, term reduction, or conditional discharge.
